SUMMARY:
This document announces that U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) will conduct a test regarding the Client Representative Technical Assistance Portal (CRTAP), a new case management system that is designed to provide a secure centralized location and standardized method for information capture, that may replace the submission of technical assistance requests by telephone or by email. This voluntary test will permit CBP to examine whether the CRTAP meets its intended use and function. This notice
(
printed page 69567)
describes the test, invites trade members to participate, and sets forth participation criteria.
DATES:
The CRTAP test will commence on December 4, 2026 and will continue for a period of 45 days, subject to any extension, modification, or termination as announced in the
Federal Register
. CBP will begin to accept requests to participate in the test on November 4, 2026, and CBP will continue to accept such requests until the CRTAP test concludes. Public comments on the test are invited and may be submitted to the address set forth below until the test commences.
ADDRESSES:
Comments and questions concerning this notice or any aspect of the test, including requests to participate in the CRTAP test, may be submitted via email to
gmb.clientrepoutreach@cpb.dhs.gov
,
with the subject line reading “Comments/Questions on CRTAP Test.”
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Mary Ann Morris, Client Services Division, Trade Transformation Office, Office of Trade, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, by email at
mary.ann.morris@cbp.dhs.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
Current Trade/Client Representative Case Management System
CBP's Client Services Representatives are located in the Office of Trade (OT), Trade Transformation Office (TTO), Client Services Division (CSD). CSD seeks to improve the stakeholder (trade user) experience through supporting the trade community's use of the Automated Commercial Environment (ACE) for processing cargo transactions, while also protecting the privacy of trade data. CSD operates and supports trade interaction within CBP electronic cargo processing systems by providing expertise for complex CBP trade processing problems. CSD oversees direct trade access into CBP's automated system and ensures the privacy of trade data. CSD is comprised of the following branches: (1) the Post Summary Processing Branch, (2) the Cargo Release and Partner Government Agency (PGA) Branch, (3) the Air and Truck Manifest Branch, (4) the Entry Summary and Post Summary Corrections (PSC) Branch, (5) the Automated Export System (AES) and Free Trade Zone (FTZ) Branch, and (6) the Ocean and Rail Manifest Branch.
Under the existing process, trade members contact their assigned CBP Client Representative by telephone or by email, requesting assistance in resolving technical issues the trade member may encounter and that the member is unable to resolve in-house. The Client Representative responds to trade inquiries and assists with resolving the issues. There is no centralized repository for the intake of this type of trade outreach and no feasible means of tracking the resolution of such matters.
II. General Description of the CRTAP Test
As part of its ongoing effort to modernize its client services trade interactions processes, CBP developed a case management system, entitled the Client Representative Technical Assistance Portal (CRTAP), to streamline operations by automating manual tasks and creating workflows, improve communication and collaboration throughout CSD and with the trade community, provide data analysis and measure the effectiveness of assistance provided to the trade community, and standardize the intake process for submission and resolution of technical issues.
The CRTAP test is a voluntary test that is limited to brokers, self-filers, software providers, Foreign Trade Zone (FTZ) Operators, Automated Export System (AES) users, and/or Automated Manifest Systems (AMS) users. CBP will select participants based on the eligibility criteria discussed in Section IV below. The selected participants will provide their requests for technical assistance to their CBP Client Representative through a designated web address linking them to the CRTAP. CBP Client Representatives will respond to the test participants through the CRTAP, requesting additional information, as needed, and ultimately resolving the technical issues. Once an issue is resolved, the CBP Client Representative will close out the transaction using the CRTAP. At the conclusion of the 45-day test period, CBP will examine any feedback received, assess the feasibility of the CRTAP, and determine whether expanded use of the portal is warranted.
The CRTAP test will commence 30 days from the date of publication of this notice in the
Federal Register
. It will continue for 45-days, unless the test is extended, modified, or discontinued in a subsequent notice published in the
Federal Register
.
CBP will continuously monitor the CRTAP, examining transactions from submission to resolution, to determine whether modifications need to be made to the test while it is ongoing. Upon conclusion of the 45-day test period, CBP will determine whether the test needs to be expanded to additional users, whether the CRTAP meets the needs of CBP and the trade, and whether the CRTAP should become a permanent case management system.
IV. Eligibility Requirements and Application Process
CBP is opening the CRTAP test to a maximum of nine (9) trade members who are brokers, self-filers, software providers, FTZ Operators, AES users, and AMS users. CBP will select a variety of participants to best evaluate the functionality of the CRTAP case management system. Interested parties should apply by submitting an email to
gmb.clientrepoutreach@cbp.dhs.gov
,
within 30 days from the date of publication of this notice, stating their interest in participating, discussing their role within the trade community, identifying their Client Representative, if one has already been assigned to them, stating how their participation will benefit them in the development of the CRTAP case management system, and acknowledging their agreement not to share any information, including CRTAP access information. Participants will be selected based on their ability to provide feedback to CBP and their role within the trade community, to ensure broad representation of the trade community. Test participants will receive technical and operational guidance throughout the test.
V. Test Evaluation Criteria
All interested parties are invited to comment on any aspect of this test. To ensure adequate feedback, test participants are required to take part in an evaluation of the test. CBP seeks comments and feedback on the design, conduct, and implementation of the test to determine whether to modify, alter, expand, limit, continue, end, or implement this program. Comments should be submitted to CBP by email to
gmb.clientrepoutreach@cbp.dhs.gov
,
with the subject line reading “Comments/Questions on CRTAP Test.”
VI. Benefits of Participating in the CRTAP Test
Participation in the test will provide test participants with the opportunity to test and give feedback to CBP on the CRTAP test design and scope. Participation may also enable test participants to determine whether submitting questions, information, and documentation through the CRTAP allows them to better track and reference communications with their CBP Client Representative, to communicate more effectively with their company clients, and to know when a given customs issue has been resolved. Ultimately, participation may
(
printed page 69568)
allow brokers, self-filers, FTZ Operators, AES users, and AMS users to determine whether the CRTAP serves as an improvement over the current process of contacting their CBP Client Representatives by telephone or email to resolve their technical assistance questions.
VII. Confidentiality
Data submitted and entered into the Client Representative Technical Assistance Portal (CRTAP) may include confidential commercial or financial information which may be protected under the Trade Secrets Act (
18 U.S.C. 1905
), the Freedom of Information Act (
5 U.S.C. 552
), or the Privacy Act (
5 U.S.C. 552a
). CBP will ensure that all Privacy Act requirements and applicable policies are adhered to during the implementation of this pilot. However, as stated in previous test notices, participation in this test or any of the previous NCAP tests is not confidential and, therefore, upon receipt of a written Freedom of Information Act request, the name(s) of an approved participant(s) will be disclosed by CBP in accordance with
5 U.S.C. 552
.
XIII. Authorization for the Test
Section 101.9(a) of title 19 of the U.S. Code of Federal Regulations (
19 CFR 101.9(a)
), provides for the general testing of programs or procedures, to evaluate the effectiveness of new technology or operational procedures. As provided in
19 CFR 101.9(a)
, for purposes of conducting a general test, the Commissioner of CBP may impose requirements different from those specified in the CBP regulations. Testing of the Client Representative Technical Assistance Portal (CRTAP) meets the requirements of
19 CFR 101.9(a)
as it involves determining whether the portal improves efficiency and reduces the burden of information collection to resolve cargo system processing issues.
IX. Paperwork Reduction Act
The Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3507(d)
) requires that CBP consider the impact of paperwork and other information collection burdens imposed on the public. An agency may not conduct or sponsor, and an individual is not required to respond to, a collection of information unless the collection of information displays a valid Office of Management and Budget (OMB) control number assigned by OMB. This CRTAP test, which is limited to nine (9) or fewer participants, is exempt from the requirements under the PRA. If CBP decides to expand the CRTAP test to additional participants, it will do so in accordance with the PRA regulations and upon publication in a future
Federal Register
Notice.

Title:
Loan Modernization Initiative.
OMB Control Number:
0570-NEW.
Summary of Collection:
Rural Development is launching the transformation of its loan and grant systems that support farmers, ranchers, and rural communities into one modern platform built for the 21st century. With a single customer file, step-by-step intake and eligibility tools, and online payments, this modern platform will manage all current active files in one place, enabling employees to deliver faster service to customers and lending partners.
To further improve customer experience and service delivery for applicants, RD is developing an Online Loan Application for the applicants to submit requests for Direct Loan assistance electronically. Future releases and iterations of the online application software will include expansion of functionality for direct loans, guarantees, and grant making and provide the ability for primary loan servicing application submission.
The use of hard copy applications will continue to be covered in the individual program information collections. However, RD will expect to further decrease the burden hours under individual OMB Control numbers as the functionality and use of the online application software expands, and more applicants shift away from using the hard copy application format.
Initial release of the online application system will be available for RBCS Business and Industry Guaranteed Loan Program and then RHS Community Facilities programs and RUS Water and Environmental Programs.
Need and Use of the Information:
The purpose of the requirements accounted for in this information collection are to ensure that the Agency has the necessary data to make sound financial decisions in regards to its programs. This data also ensures that program funds go only to eligible applicants and projects and allows the Agency to track that recipients stay eligible in accordance with program regulations.
Additionally, to abide by
2 CFR 180.405
&
2 CFR 180.425(b)
, the Principal of every application will need to supply their SSN to ensure Do Not Pay can be complied with. If the specified principal is not present in the organization's structure, select the highest-ranking executive responsible for the organization's financial operations, fiscal health, and long term financial strategy. Background
The FAA issued AD 2025-20-02, Amendment 39-23155 (
90 FR 53208

AD 2025-20-02 was prompted by EASA AD 2024-0240, dated December 10, 2024 (EASA AD 2024-0240), issued by EASA, which is the Technical Agent for the Member States of the European Union. EASA issued EASA AD 2024-0240, dated December 10, 2024 (EASA AD 2024-0240), to address an unsafe condition identified as an occurrence of an inaccurate flight director calculation on approach. The MCAI stated that heading splits can cause errors in the flight director calculations, which results in lateral offsets to the desired approach course. The FAA issued AD 2025-20-02 as an interim action to address the unsafe condition described above.
AD 2025-20-02 requires incorporating a temporary revision into the existing AFM for the affected
(
printed page 69507)
airplanes, which revises the Abnormal Procedures Section.
Actions Since AD 2025-20-02 Was Issued
Since the FAA issued AD 2025-20-02, EASA superseded EASA AD 2024-0240 and issued EASA AD 2026-0149, dated July 28, 2026 (EASA AD 2026-0149) (also referred to as the MCAI). The MCAI states that, since EASA AD 2024-0240 was issued, Pilatus developed Primus APEX DFZ Build 6.0 software and issued service information providing instructions for installing the software. Pilatus also issued AFM-TR 02371-081, which provides operational instructions applicable after installation of Primus APEX DFZ Build 6.0 software.
The MCAI retains the requirement to incorporate the existing AFM instructions and adds requirements to install the updated software and, after installation of the updated software, incorporate the revised operational instructions into the AFM. The FAA is issuing this AD to prevent heading splits that can cause errors in flight director calculations, resulting in lateral offsets to the desired approach course. The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in an increased pilot workload and a reduction of the safety margins.

These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority (CAA) of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. I. Policy Objectives
The policy objective of the proposal is to rebalance the FDIC's framework for making prompt deposit insurance determinations in the event of a failure of a large insured depository institution (IDI). Specifically, the proposal would remove
12 CFR part 370
, the FDIC's rule entitled “Recordkeeping for Timely Deposit Insurance Determination” (part 370), and no longer require IDIs subject to that rule to configure their information technology systems (IT systems) to be capable of calculating deposit insurance coverage, while preserving measures intended to enable the FDIC to calculate deposit insurance coverage for such IDIs “as soon as possible” in the event of their failure.
[
1
]
The FDIC also proposes to amend
12 CFR 360.9
, the FDIC's rule entitled “Large-Bank Deposit Insurance Determination Modernization” (§ 360.9) in order to improve the FDIC's ability to meet its statutory obligations, particularly its obligation to pay deposit insurance as soon as possible either by cash or by making available to each depositor a transferred deposit in a new insured depository institution.
[
2
]
This proposed amendment would not add additional burden or affect the requirements applicable to IDIs currently subject to § 360.9, but would, among other things, require an IDI having at least $2 billion in deposits and two million or more deposit accounts (generally, IDIs currently subject to part 370) to maintain and provide to the FDIC certain depositor and customer data needed for the FDIC to calculate deposit insurance in the event of the IDI's failure.
[
3
]
Since first adopting part 370 in 2016, the FDIC has enhanced its own systems and capabilities related to calculating deposit insurance and making deposit insurance determinations. The FDIC believes that with this improvement to
(
printed page 69643)
its internal capacity, the FDIC can reduce regulatory burden by rescinding part 370 without materially impeding the FDIC's ability to calculate deposit insurance. Part 370 is generally a more burdensome regulatory framework than § 360.9, especially for new entrants to part 370, who must build and maintain their own IT systems capable of calculating deposit insurance in-house and maintain a broader set of information in deposit account records than is required under § 360.9.
II. Background
A. Section 360.9
When the FDIC began the rulemaking process to develop the current § 360.9, the FDIC recognized that the increased number of deposit accounts, greater geographic dispersion of depositors, more diversity of data systems, and potential data consistency challenges at larger institutions created challenges for the FDIC in conducting a deposit insurance determination in the event of failure. In addition, the FDIC understood that the process of deposit insurance determination was inherently complex and dependent upon the complete and accurate deposit account records of the failed IDI. Consistent with the statutory requirement to provide access to insured deposits “as soon as possible,” the FDIC has typically been able to allow most depositors access to their insured deposits on the next business day after a bank's failure. In an effort to maintain this standard, the FDIC began considering new methods to modernize the deposit insurance determination process and stated in a 2005 advance notice of proposed rulemaking (ANPR) that its goals were to “minimize disruption to depositors and communities, and maximize recoveries” for the Deposit Insurance Fund (DIF) in the event of a failure of a large IDI.
[
4
]
The FDIC considered the limitations of its then current processes in light of the larger institutions resulting from mergers and internal growth.
The 2005 ANPR requested comment on options for enhancing the speed at which depositors at more complex IDIs would receive access to their funds in the event of failure.
[
5
]
In response to public comment, the FDIC published a second ANPR focusing on less costly and less burdensome alternatives.
[
6
]
In January 2008, the FDIC then published a notice of proposed rulemaking composed of two parts addressing (1) issues involving the FDIC's practices for determining deposit and other liability account balances at a failed IDI, and (2) a requirement for certain IDIs to adopt mechanisms that would, in the event of the IDI's failure, provide the FDIC with standard depositor and customer information and allow the FDIC to place and release holds on liability accounts, including deposits.
[
7
]
In July 2008, the FDIC adopted a final rule in a form similar to the proposal.
[
8
]
Currently, § 360.9 applies only to an IDI if, based on its Reports of Condition and Income (Call Report), it has at least $2 billion in deposits and at least either: 250,000 deposit accounts or $20 billion in total assets, regardless of the number of deposit accounts (these IDIs are defined as “covered institutions” in § 360.9).
[
9
]
Section 360.9 requires covered institutions to have in place mechanisms that would, in the event of the IDI's failure, provide the FDIC with depositor and customer information in a standard data format and allow the automated placement and release of provisional holds on liability accounts, including deposits.
[
10
]
The FDIC's ability to provide depositors prompt access to insured deposits and determine the insurance status of depositors in a failed IDI in a timely manner is a critical element for ensuring a least-costly resolution and maintaining public confidence. The requirements of § 360.9 provide essential support for the FDIC to meet its statutory obligations, including paying deposit insurance “as soon as possible” following the failure of an IDI and resolving the IDI in the manner least costly to the DIF.
[
11
]
The FDIC believes that the proposed amendments to § 360.9 will help the FDIC to continue to meet these objectives, especially for larger and more complex IDIs.
B. Part 370
In 2015, the FDIC issued an ANPR seeking comment on whether certain IDIs such as those that have two million or more deposit accounts should be required to take steps to ensure that depositors would have access to their FDIC-insured funds in a timely manner (usually within one business day after failure) if one of these institutions were to fail.
[
12
]
Specifically, the FDIC sought comment on whether these IDIs should be required to enhance their recordkeeping to maintain, and be able to provide, substantially more accurate and complete data on each depositor's ownership interest by right and capacity for all, or a large subset, of the institution's deposit accounts. The FDIC also sought comment on whether these IDIs' IT systems should have the capability to calculate the insured and uninsured amounts for each depositor by deposit insurance category for all, or a substantial subset of, deposit accounts at the end of any business day. The FDIC then published in the
Federal Register
a notice of proposed rulemaking,
[
13
]
considered all of the comments received, and adopted a final rule in 2016 to facilitate prompt payment of FDIC-insured deposits when IDIs with two million or more deposit accounts fail.
[
14
]
This 2016 final rule required each IDI that has two million or more deposit accounts to configure its IT system to be capable of calculating deposit insurance in the event of the IDI's failure and maintain complete and accurate information needed by the FDIC to determine deposit insurance coverage with respect to each deposit account. These IDIs were released from the requirements of § 360.9 upon complying with the requirements of part 370.
In April 2019, the FDIC issued a notice of proposed rulemaking soliciting public comment on its proposal to make certain substantive revisions to part 370 to clarify the requirements, better align its burdens with its benefits, and make technical changes.
[
15
]
The FDIC then promulgated a final rule seeking to address many of the issues identified by commenters regarding components of part 370 that were unclear or unduly burdensome.
[
16
]
Part 370 requires each IDI that has two million or more deposit accounts to develop its IT systems to be capable of calculating the insured and uninsured amount in each deposit account by ownership right and capacity, which would be used by the FDIC to make deposit insurance determinations in the event of the IDI's failure.
[
17
]
Part 370 also requires these IDIs to maintain complete and accurate information needed by the FDIC to determine deposit insurance coverage with respect to each deposit account.
[
18
]
However, alternative recordkeeping standards are permitted for certain types of accounts for which the covered institution does not otherwise maintain complete information needed for a
(
printed page 69644)
deposit insurance determination.
[
19
]
Part 370 also prescribes the file types, data fields, and allowable values the IDIs' IT systems must produce.
[
20
]
Additionally, part 370 provides for regular certification of compliance and periodic FDIC compliance testing.
[
21
]
Once an IDI submits its compliance certification under part 370, it is automatically released from having to comply with § 360.9.
[
22
]
The FDIC adopted part 370 to enhance the FDIC's ability to pay deposit insurance “as soon as possible” as required under section 11(f) of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act (FDI Act) for these larger and more complex IDIs. Though section 11(f) of the FDI Act does not specify a time limit for paying insured deposits, the FDIC strives to pay deposit insurance promptly after an IDI failure and expects to make most insured deposits available by the next business day after IDI failure.
[
23
]
The FDIC adopted part 370 to address concerns that, at the time of an IDI's failure, deposit account records and data may be inconsistent, incomplete, or otherwise insufficient to support timely and accurate deposit insurance determinations. The rule also was intended to mitigate limitations in FDIC systems to process the volume of accounts associated with the failure of a large IDI. To address these concerns, part 370 requires covered institutions to develop and maintain the recordkeeping and information technology capabilities necessary to support the FDIC's resolution functions in the event of failure. The dual problems of incomplete depositor records and a much larger and more complex IDI could result in deposit insurance determinations being significantly delayed, particularly if a very large IDI fails with little warning.
[
24
]
As discussed below, the FDIC believes that the significant advancements in the FDIC's capabilities and systems, together with planned expansion of those capabilities, have improved the FDIC's ability to promptly determine deposit insurance coverage for depositors of large and complex failed IDIs to the point that, when coupled with the requirements in the proposed revised § 360.9, the FDIC would be able to perform the deposit insurance determination promptly without the need for the requirements set forth in part 370.
III. Rescission of Part 370
The FDIC is proposing to remove and reserve part 370 of the FDIC's regulations. The FDIC believes that advancements in the FDIC's own capabilities and systems related to deposit insurance determinations render it unnecessary for the largest IDIs to build and maintain their own IT systems capable of calculating deposit insurance coverage if they comply with the provisions of § 360.9 as outlined in this proposal. When combined with the revision of § 360.9 as outlined in this proposal, part 370 can therefore be removed from the FDIC's regulations without materially impeding the FDIC's ability to calculate deposit insurance. The FDIC believes that removing part 370 would also reduce the net burden on the IDIs currently subject to part 370. For example, these IDIs will no longer have to maintain certain depositor and customer data and operate, maintain, continuously enhance, and remediate deficiencies in their IT systems to be capable of calculating deposit insurance coverage within 24 hours after the appointment of the FDIC as receiver.
[
25
]
As described in greater detail below, specified recordkeeping requirements for certain deposit account information under part 370 would be preserved for larger and more complex IDIs under the proposal.
[
26
]

IV. Amendments to Section 360.9
A. Scope and Purpose
The FDIC is undertaking this notice of proposed rulemaking to amend § 360.9. Section 360.9 would apply to all IDIs that have at least $2 billion in deposits and at least either: 250,000 deposit accounts; or $20 billion in total assets, regardless of the number of deposit accounts (covered institutions). The proposal would add a new defined term, larger covered institution, to § 360.9. A larger covered institution would be defined as a covered institution with at least $2 billion in deposits and two million or more deposit accounts.
[
28
]
The proposal would, among other things:
Apply the requirements of § 360.9 to larger covered institutions;
Require larger covered institutions to collect and maintain complete and accurate depositor and customer data for certain mandatory data fields unless otherwise provided for;
Provide for a larger covered institution to request an exemption from the standard data requirements;
Include a safe harbor provision for covered institutions that have submitted a request for exemption or extension while awaiting the FDIC's response;
Provide for automatic release from the requirements of § 360.9 if it falls below the covered institution threshold for three consecutive quarters;
Clarify the definition of foreign deposits and related terminology to conform with
12 CFR part 330
; and
Make corrections and technical and conforming changes.
The proposal would index, but not otherwise change, the thresholds for an IDI to become a covered institution. The proposal would neither include any new requirement nor impose any additional burden on any IDI currently subject to § 360.9.
The FDIC proposes to include IDIs that are currently subject to part 370 within the scope of the revised § 360.9 to facilitate prompt payment of FDIC-insured deposits should one of these institutions fail and to reduce compliance burdens for these IDIs. As noted above, these IDIs would no longer be required to operate and maintain IT systems capable of promptly calculating deposit insurance coverage, as the FDIC would instead rely on its own internal IT system to calculate deposit insurance. These IDIs would also become subject to the recordkeeping
(
printed page 69645)
and provisional hold requirements of § 360.9 if revised as proposed.

B. Modified and New Definitions
Section 360.9(b) contains the definition of terms used throughout § 360.9. The proposal would add or revise the following definitions:
Deposit.
The term “deposit” would be added as a defined term and would have the same meaning as provided under section 3(
l

12 U.S.C. 1813
(
l

Deposit account records.
The term “deposit account records” would be added as a defined term and would have the meaning given that term in
12 CFR 330.1(e)
.
Foreign deposits and related terminology.
The FDIC proposes to revise the definition of foreign deposits and add new definitions for “dually payable deposit,” “domestic deposit,” “domestic deposit account,” and “foreign deposit account.” Subsequent to the promulgation of the current § 360.9, the FDIC clarified the treatment of liabilities in foreign offices of U.S. IDIs for the purpose of insurance coverage and priority in resolution.
[
29
]
That rulemaking clarified the treatment of a “dually payable deposit,” which is a liability held in a foreign office of a U.S. IDI that (1) would be a deposit if carried on the books and records of the IDI in the United States and (2) is expressly payable in the United States. Such dually payable deposits receive treatment as deposits for purposes of priority in resolution, but do not receive deposit insurance coverage. Under this proposed rulemaking, “foreign deposits” would include any dually payable deposit together with any liability held in a foreign office of a U.S. IDI that (1) would be a deposit if carried on the books and records of the IDI in the United States and (2) is not expressly payable in the United States. Foreign deposits that are not dually payable are not treated as deposits for purposes of priority in resolution and do not receive deposit insurance coverage.
The term “domestic deposit” in this proposal would be defined as any deposit other than a dually payable deposit. New definitions have also been added for “deposit account,” “domestic deposit account,” and “foreign deposit account.” These new and revised terms correspond to reporting requirements throughout the rule, including in § 360.9(c), “Posting and removing provisional holds;” Appendix C, “Deposit File Structure;” and Appendix D, “Sweep/Automated Credit Account File Structure.” The distinction between domestic deposits, foreign deposits, domestic deposit accounts, and foreign deposit accounts is intended to correspond to how covered institutions maintain their deposits and deposit accounts within the United States and at foreign offices, and therefore how covered institutions can most easily report on such activities for purposes of Appendices C and D.
Transactional features.
The term “transactional features” would be added as a defined term and would have substantively the same meaning as the definition contained in
12 CFR 370.2(j)
. Transactional features with respect to a deposit account would mean that the account holder or the beneficial owner of deposits can make a transfer from the deposit account to a party other than the account holder, beneficial owner of deposits, or the larger covered institution itself, by a method that may result in such transfer being reflected in the end-of-day ledger balance for such deposit account on a day that is later than the day that such transfer is initiated, even if initiated prior to the larger covered institution's normal cutoff time for such transaction. A deposit account also has transactional features if preauthorized or automatic instructions provide for transfer of deposits in the deposit account to another deposit account at the same institution, if such other deposit account itself has transactional features. Notwithstanding the proposed rescission of part 370, the FDIC continues to recognize the importance of timely deposit insurance determinations for accounts with transactional features and proposes to require larger covered institutions to take actions for certain deposit accounts with transactional features, as discussed in Section IV.E.
Account holder.
The term “account holder” would be added as a defined term and would have the same meaning as in
12 CFR 370.2(a)
, and would, therefore, mean the person or entity who has opened a deposit account with a covered institution and with whom the covered institution has a direct legal and contractual relationship with respect to the deposit.
The proposal would make technical edits to the definitions, including “covered institution” and “international banking facility deposit” (IBF deposit), but these changes would not substantively affect the definitions or the requirements of § 360.9.

C. Posting and Removing Provisional Holds
The proposal would not change any of the provisional hold requirements of § 360.9 for covered institutions. However, the proposal would require IDIs currently subject to part 370 to transition to complying with § 360.9. Therefore, the proposal would require larger covered institutions to be able to place and remove provisional holds in the manner specified under § 360.9.
One of the FDIC's chief objectives in adopting § 360.9 was to require covered institutions to develop a mechanism to facilitate the FDIC's ability to provide liquidity to the failed bank's depositors soon after the IDI's failure while the FDIC completed its deposit insurance determinations. All IDIs currently subject to part 370 that would become larger covered institutions were previously subject to the requirements of § 360.9 and therefore should be familiar with this requirement. However, since becoming part 370 covered institutions, these larger institutions have not been required to maintain the provisional hold capabilities required under § 360.9.

30

When the FDIC adopted part 370, the FDIC did not retain the provisional hold requirements for part 370 IDIs in light of the facts that (1) IDIs covered by part 370 would be subject to substantial additional burden to develop and maintain IT systems capable of calculating deposit insurance and (2) the FDIC believed provisional hold
(
printed page 69646)

However, under part 370, IDIs still are not able to calculate deposit insurance for all accounts promptly upon failure, suggesting that provisional hold capabilities may still be relevant. Section 360.9 requires a covered institution to have in place practices and procedures to provide the FDIC with depositor and customer data in a standard format following the close of any day's business. Consistent with the description in the 2008 final rule preamble, the FDIC expects the depositor and customer data to be provided as soon as practicable, but no later than the following calendar day, and to reflect the end-of-day ledger balances customarily shown on the covered institution's books and records as of the day the data are requested.

The standard data files are created through a mapping of pre-existing data elements and internal institution codes into standard data formats.”

Under § 360.9, covered institutions must provide the depositor and customer data in the required standard data format prescribed by the FDIC if the covered institution has the information, but it does not need to collect this information if it does not already maintain it. Data is to be provided on all non-closed domestic deposit accounts or foreign deposit accounts as well as sweep account arrangements and automated credit account arrangements. Under the proposal, the data files still must be provided to the FDIC in the most expeditious manner. Additional data that may be helpful to the FDIC's deposit insurance determination process but not required by the regulation may also be provided by a covered institution.
Larger covered institutions would be required to comply with additional standard data requirements; specifically, 26 data fields would be mandatory for these IDIs. These data fields are the ones that are most critical for the FDIC to conduct a prompt deposit insurance determination. Of the 26 data fields, 21 fields are currently required to be populated in the part 370 output files. The remaining five mandatory data fields are currently included in § 360.9 but are not explicitly required by part 370. Considering that part 370 generally requires banks to maintain complete and accurate information needed to calculate deposit insurance coverage with respect to each deposit account except as otherwise provided in the rule, the FDIC expects that larger covered institutions already have this information readily available as part of their customary banking operations. These five data fields are: (1) deposit type indicator (domestic vs foreign deposit); (2) customer ownership indicator at the account level (which is very similar to a part 370 requirement); (3) account title (as titled on the bank records); (4) relationship code to identify how customers are related to the account; and (5) beneficiary code to identify the type of account used for agent, custodian, or trustee relationships. Overall, the FDIC expects that the aggregate data reporting requirements under revised § 360.9 would be materially less burdensome than under part 370.
These mandatory data fields would be required only for larger covered institutions under the proposal.

E. Actions Required by Larger Covered Institutions for Certain Deposit Accounts With Transactional Features
The proposal would require that larger covered institutions take certain actions reasonably calculated to ensure that account holders who have certain types of deposit accounts with transactional features are aware of the requirement to promptly provide to the FDIC the information needed for the FDIC to calculate deposit insurance with respect to each of those accounts in the event of the larger covered institution's failure. This proposed requirement would be similar to the requirement set forth in
12 CFR 370.5
, but it would be less burdensome and narrower in scope. Its focus would be on providing depositors instruction for claiming deposit insurance. It would not obligate larger covered institutions to validate data format and delivery capabilities. Larger covered institutions could satisfy the proposed requirement by either (1) making a good faith effort to enter into contractual arrangements with the account holder that obligate the account holder to deliver information needed for deposit insurance calculation to the FDIC in a format prescribed in a new Appendix I of part 360 within 24 hours after the appointment of the FDIC as receiver; or (2) providing the account holder with a written disclosure specifying the information and format requirements of new Appendix I to part 360 and stating that, if the larger covered institution fails and the FDIC is appointed receiver, then the account holder might not have access to deposits before the account holder delivers information to the FDIC in the format prescribed in that new appendix. Although part 370 currently requires both actions, the FDIC believes that a less burdensome requirement focused on informing these account holders that they will likely need to provide additional information to the FDIC in a predefined format in order for the FDIC to make prompt payment of deposit insurance, and that access to deposit insurance may be limited before that information is provided, would be sufficient. These actions are intended to inform larger covered institutions' account holders that the process for calculating deposit insurance can be dependent upon receipt of information that is not in the larger covered institutions' deposit account records and production of that information to the FDIC is the account holder's responsibility. New Appendix I would be added to part 360 to demonstrate the deposit information and format for submission to the FDIC. Larger covered institutions would be required to include or reference the elements of Appendix I in their agreements with, or disclosures to, account holders who have accounts with transactional features.
This requirement would be limited to certain types of deposit accounts with “transactional features” because prompt calculation and payment of deposit insurance on those deposit accounts is vital to orderly payment processing. Delays to deposit insurance calculation and payment on those deposit accounts could delay or disrupt the payment instruction clearing and settlement process for “in flight” transactions. If depositors are aware of this fact and are proactive in facilitating the FDIC's prompt payment of deposit insurance, then this disruption could be minimized. That is the intent of this proposed requirement.
New Appendix I would be completed by account holders who hold deposits on behalf of others (
e.g.,
a deposit broker, a deposit placement service, or some other agent who acts in a representative capacity for the beneficial owner of the deposit) and who expect their deposit accounts to be insured on a pass-through basis. Appendix I would be filled out by the account holder (not
(
printed page 69648)
by the IDI) and only in the event of failure. The FDIC anticipates that, for these deposit accounts, there will be a full set of subaccounts represented in Appendix I naming the beneficial owners of deposits in the account.

12 CFR 330.14

12 CFR 330.10

12 CFR 330.12

The FDIC believes that the account holders who have authority and control over these types of accounts have a responsibility to the principals for whom they serve as agents to diligently maintain records of deposit ownership in good faith and in the regular course of business, and to understand the conditions for FDIC deposit insurance coverage sufficiently to take the actions needed to claim deposit insurance promptly.

F. Implementation Requirements
Section 360.9 currently provides that an institution must comply with the requirements of § 360.9 no later than 18 months following the end of the second calendar quarter for which it meets the criteria to be a covered institution. The proposal would generally maintain this 18-month implementation timeframe for institutions that become covered institutions. Any IDI that is a larger covered institution as of the effective date of the revised rule would be required to comply with (1) all requirements of § 360.9 other than the provisional hold requirements no later than six months after the effective date of the revised rule and (2) the provisional hold requirements within 18 months after the effective date of the revised rule. An IDI that is not a covered institution as of the effective date of the final rule and that becomes a larger covered institution after the effective date of the final rule would be given an 18-month implementation period following the end of the second calendar quarter for which it meets the criteria for a larger covered institution.
The FDIC is proposing that, for IDIs that (1) became covered institutions before the effective date of the final rule and (2) have a compliance date that occurs after the effective date of the final rule, the 18-month implementation period would not be shortened or extended as a consequence of a revision of § 360.9. Each such covered institution would be required to comply with the requirements of § 360.9 no later than 18 months following the end of the second calendar quarter for which it met the criteria for a covered institution because the proposal would not impose any new requirement on such an IDI. The FDIC also does not expect that any of these covered institutions would become a larger covered institution as of the effective date if § 360.9 is revised as proposed. However, such IDIs would be permitted to submit an extension request, as described below.
The proposal would provide a 12-month implementation period to a covered institution that becomes a larger covered institution after meeting the larger covered institution threshold for two consecutive quarters. The FDIC understands that it may take time for such a covered institution to obtain the additional information required for the mandatory data fields and to take actions required for certain deposit accounts with transactional features, as described in Section IV.E. The FDIC believes that one year would be sufficient time for a covered institution to comply with these requirements after becoming a larger covered institution. Most covered institutions already provide the information for the mandatory data fields, so the FDIC does not expect the transition to be a significant burden. The FDIC also believes that no implementation time would be needed for a larger covered institution to adjust its compliance efforts after the number of its deposit accounts falls below two million accounts because the larger covered institution would already be complying with the requirements of § 360.9.

Covered institutions may request that the FDIC extend the deadline for complying with the requirements of § 360.9. Covered institutions may also submit a request for an exemption from certain of the automated provisional hold requirements.

Additionally, § 360.9 allows a covered institution to request an exemption from its requirements if the institution has a high concentration of deposits incidental to credit card operations.

The proposal would not change these exemption provisions or previously granted exemptions. Any covered institution can submit such requests, including larger covered institutions.
The FDIC is aware of the challenges IDIs subject to part 370 experienced in obtaining missing depositor information and complying with part 370's recordkeeping requirements. The FDIC intends to publish certain existing applicable part 370 frequently asked questions as § 360.9 guidance that would address some of these challenges for larger covered institutions. The FDIC also proposes to enable larger covered institutions to seek relief where necessary and appropriate in the form of a full or partial exemption from the requirements of § 360.9(d)(1) for a relatively small number of accounts if circumstances exist that would make it impracticable or overly burdensome to meet those requirements with respect to certain types of accounts. As with any exemption request, the FDIC would consider such requests on a case-by-case basis in light of the objectives of the rule.
With respect to covered institutions, including larger covered institutions, that submit a request for an exemption or extension, the proposal would provide that such covered institutions would not be considered to be noncompliant with § 360.9 with regard to the requirements from which relief is sought while awaiting the FDIC's response to such request. The FDIC intends to respond to such requests promptly and covered institutions would not be penalized while a request for relief is pending.
Section 360.9 currently does not have a codified provision that releases an IDI from the requirements of § 360.9 when it no longer satisfies the criteria to be a covered institution. The FDIC has been notifying IDIs when they fall below the threshold for a covered institution for three consecutive quarters that they are no longer subject to the requirements of § 360.9. The proposal would codify a provision that would automatically release a covered institution from the requirements of § 360.9 if it does not meet the criteria to be a covered institution for three consecutive quarters. Moreover, the proposal would automatically release a larger covered institution from the additional requirements of § 360.9(d)(1)(ii) and (iii) and (d)(5) if it does not meet the criteria to be a larger covered institution for three consecutive quarters. The FDIC would not expect a larger covered institution to be released directly from the requirements of § 360.9 without first becoming a covered institution. The FDIC believes that a covered institution's release after three quarters of not meeting the criteria to be a covered institution would provide greater certainty that the institution will remain below the threshold for coverage. From past experience with both § 360.9 and part 370, the FDIC is aware of circumstances in which an IDI has moved in and out of scope of one of these rules over the course of one or two quarters. The FDIC may still inform a covered institution when it is released but the release would occur automatically regardless.
Like any other IDI, an institution released under § 360.9(j)(1) could become a covered institution again if it were to have at least $2 billion in deposits and at least either 250,000 deposit accounts, or $20 billion in total assets (regardless of the number of deposit accounts), for two consecutive quarters. Similarly, a covered institution released under § 360.9(j)(2) from the additional requirements applicable to larger covered institutions could become subject to those requirements again if it were to have at least $2 billion in deposits and two million or more deposit accounts for two consecutive quarters.

H. Records Retention
Alongside the proposal, the FDIC intends to change its practice with respect to retaining depositor and customer data that it receives from covered institutions, including larger covered institutions, in connection with the FDIC's § 360.9 compliance reviews. Currently, this data is retained by the FDIC for each covered institution until the next § 360.9 compliance review. The FDIC has maintained this data to compare results from previous compliance reviews and to assist the FDIC in having baseline data in the event of a covered institution's failure. For part 370 compliance tests, the FDIC has been retaining deposit account data up to 120 days after providing testing results via the final management letter, with most data being deleted in practice within 60 days of distribution of the
(
printed page 69650)
letter. Once deleted, the FDIC maintains a summary of the data to support the testing results.
The FDIC recognizes the importance of minimizing the volume of sensitive information it holds and ensuring that it only holds such information when needed. As a result, first, effective immediately, the FDIC will fully delete all depositor and customer data no later than 60 days following a § 360.9 or part 370 compliance review. The FDIC believes that this would reduce the risks and sensitivity associated with maintaining sensitive information while still providing the FDIC with the opportunity to validate results for purposes of achieving the goal of prompt deposit insurance determinations.
Second, the FDIC will no longer require covered institutions to provide the FDIC with customers' social security and tax identification numbers (SSN/TINs) in connection with § 360.9 compliance reviews, given the highly sensitive nature of such information. Instead, the FDIC would assign synthetic SSN/TINs to each individual customer, to replicate the FDIC's deposit insurance determination process. The FDIC would then validate the bank's process of assigning unique customer identification numbers to ensure that individual customers are each assigned one unique identification number.
The FDIC will also, upon request, engage with covered institutions on a bilateral basis to address any additional concerns related to sensitive information.
The FDIC invites comments on all aspects of data retention for § 360.9 compliance reviews. In particular, the FDIC seeks comment on the following:
(23) Should the FDIC consider a different approach to the retention of depositor and customer data in connection with FDIC conducted § 360.9 compliance reviews for covered institutions and larger covered institutions? If so, in what aspects and why?
I. Indexing Thresholds
The FDIC proposes to index the dollar amounts used in the definitions of covered institution and larger covered institution. As noted by the FDIC previously, the use of thresholds allows the FDIC to differentiate and tailor regulatory requirements based on an institution's size, risk profile, and level of complexity. However, static dollar-based thresholds can lead to unintended policy consequences if threshold levels are not periodically updated or indexed to inflation. For this reason, the proposal would provide for indexing of the baseline dollar threshold to be a covered institution and a larger covered institution. This is consistent with the FDIC's agency-wide initiative to index dollar values in the FDIC's Rules and Regulations to ensure the FDIC's regulatory expectations are appropriately tailored.
The thresholds would also be measured from a baseline date. The baseline date would be the effective date on which the proposal becomes a final rule. The first adjustment would be effective on October 1, 2029. Thereafter, biennial adjustments would be effective on October 1 following each consecutive two-year period ending on August 30. Adjustments would be calculated by multiplying the applicable baseline threshold value by one plus the cumulative percentage change in the non-seasonally adjusted Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W). An annual adjustment would occur if the non-seasonally adjusted CPI-W increased by more than 8 percent over the 12-month period ending August 30 of the year following the year in which the most recent adjustment was made. No adjustment would be made if multiplying the applicable baseline threshold by one plus the cumulative percentage change in non-seasonally adjusted CPI-W from the applicable baseline date, and rounding the result as prescribed, would not increase the then-current threshold.
Under the proposal, the FDIC generally would announce threshold adjustments pursuant to the indexing methodology by publishing a final rule in the
Federal Register
. Such final rules would amend the Code of Federal Regulations to reflect the adjusted thresholds for the definitions of covered institution and larger covered institution and would not be subject to a notice and comment period. Although the FDIC would fully expect to publish a final rule in the
Federal Register
, the adjustment would occur even in the absence of a publication in the
Federal Register
.
The FDIC invites comments on all aspects of indexing in the proposal. In particular, the FDIC seeks comment on the following aspects of the proposal:
(24) Should the proposed rule index the dollar amounts for purposes of the definitions of covered institution and larger covered institution in the proposed rule? Why or why not? Should the FDIC consider alternate approaches for indexing these definitions?
V. Expected Effects
A. Introduction and Baseline Assumptions
As discussed above, the proposal would rescind part 370, subject larger covered institutions to the requirements of § 360.9, and clarify certain § 360.9 requirements to reduce regulatory burden and relieve larger covered institutions of the requirements to build and maintain deposit insurance calculation systems. The FDIC estimates the impact of these proposed changes by comparing economic outcomes under the proposal relative to a baseline in which the proposal is not adopted and the current regulations are in effect. For its estimates under both the proposal and the baseline, the FDIC is utilizing all other relevant laws and regulations in effect, as well as the financial and economic conditions of affected entities, as of March 31, 2026.
Although not all of the effects of the proposal can be quantified, the analysis provides monetary estimates of the most material effects based on current and historical labor burden estimates for part 370 and § 360.9.
[
39 40

To convert labor burden (as measured in hours) to 2026 dollars, the FDIC uses an estimated labor compensation rate of $125 per hour.
[
41

Given that the most material effects of the proposal would fall upon IDIs that are currently subject to part 370 (part 370 IDIs), much of the discussion will focus on the quantified effects on this group of IDIs. To account for the variation of compliance costs across IDIs, this analysis classifies each part 370 IDI as either a Lowest Complexity, Middle Complexity, or Highest Complexity IDI.

]
This
(
printed page 69651)

The FDIC analyzes the monetized effects of the proposal, relative to the baseline, over a 10-year period. The 10-year analysis horizon is sufficiently long to illustrate the net expected effects of the proposal, while avoiding potential uncertainties related to future economic conditions that may arise with longer time horizons.
Given the uncertainties involved in estimating costs and benefits to IDIs across a 10-year horizon, this analysis assumes the financial conditions of affected IDIs are fixed to those reported as of the quarter ending March 31, 2026. In addition, any new IDI qualifying for part 370 under the baseline is assumed to be a Lowest Complexity IDI under the baseline and the proposal and to maintain those conditions throughout the 10-year period. To the extent that this assumption is violated and deposit accounts grow, the estimates of burden under the baseline would be larger than estimated, and the resulting cost savings would be higher than estimated. As such, this assumption provides a conservative estimate of the monetized cost savings provided by the proposal.
This section also discusses the qualitative effects of the proposal on all affected institutions, as well as on the FDIC, the DIF, and the public at large.

D. Effects on Covered Institutions, the Deposit Insurance Fund, and Depositors
In addition to the effects on current part 370 IDIs described above, the proposal would have effects on all covered institutions, the DIF, and depositors.
The proposal would revise certain provisions in § 360.9 to clarify definitions and codify existing practices. These revisions are expected to provide modest benefits to covered institutions. Covered institutions may pass along some or all of the cost savings provided by the proposal to their customers through lower fees or higher deposit interest rates.
Direct costs of the proposal on covered institutions include minor updates of systems or practices to align with the proposed revisions. While it is difficult to quantify these effects, the FDIC expects that these effects are much less material than the effects discussed above.
If the proposal were to result in delays in insurance determinations in the event of the failure of a part 370 IDI, this would result in indirect costs. Any such delay may result in either inaccurate deposit insurance payouts, which could lead to a loss in the DIF, or prolongation of the waiting period before the payouts, which could lead to disruptions for account holders and a loss in consumer confidence. However, such an outcome would be highly unlikely under the proposal; since part 370 was adopted in 2016, the FDIC has significantly enhanced its own claims processing and deposit insurance determination capabilities, so the FDIC can now readily process many more insurance determinations than it could in 2016. In addition, the proposed requirements for larger covered institutions in § 360.9 would incorporate those requirements in part 370 most critical to such insurance determinations.
E. Indexing Thresholds
The proposal would index the dollar amounts in § 360.9. The indexing provision would preserve the level of thresholds set forth in the proposed rule in real dollar terms, thereby avoiding the undesirable and unintended outcome where the asset threshold changes due solely to inflation rather than actual changes in an institution's size, risk profile, or level of complexity.
F. Conclusion
Based on the analysis described above, the FDIC has determined that the expected benefits of the proposal justify its expected costs. The FDIC invites comments on all aspects of the supporting information provided in this analysis, and, in particular, whether the proposal would have any material effects that the FDIC has not identified.
VI. Alternatives Considered
The FDIC considered alternatives to the proposal to meet the objectives of this rulemaking. For the reasons described below, the FDIC views the proposal as the most appropriate and effective means of achieving the policy objectives described in Section I. The FDIC considered not promulgating any regulatory action to amend § 360.9 and rescind part 370. As previously discussed, however, the FDIC has determined that the rescission of part 370 and amendment to § 360.9 would reduce regulatory burden for IDIs subject to part 370 while maintaining measures that facilitate the FDIC's ability to promptly make a deposit insurance determination by relying on its own IT systems to accurately calculate deposit insurance. As discussed above, the proposal would provide cost savings and other benefits relative to this no-action alternative.
The FDIC also considered modifying the threshold for coverage under § 360.9 but concluded that the requirements of § 360.9 promote the FDIC's ability to meet its statutory obligations in resolving institutions covered at the current thresholds. The FDIC considered requiring all the data fields in Appendices C through G of part 360 as mandatory for all covered institutions. The FDIC did not pursue this approach because it believes the benefits would not outweigh the additional burdens on covered institutions. The FDIC has determined that the proposal strikes an appropriate balance by removing the requirement for an IDI subject to part 370 to maintain an IT system to calculate deposit insurance and enhancing the FDIC's ability to meet its statutory obligation to pay deposit insurance “as soon as possible” following failure. The proposal would help enable the FDIC to resolve IDIs subject to § 360.9 in the manner least costly to the DIF by preserving franchise value through prompt deposit insurance determination and maintenance of continuity of a failed covered institution's deposit operations.
The FDIC invites comments on all possible alternatives to the proposal and will reconsider all of its preliminary determinations in the proposal after review of comments.

§ 314.1
Threshold indexing
(a)
Methodology.
The dollar thresholds specified in paragraph (c) of this section shall be adjusted by multiplying the baseline threshold values specified in paragraph (c) of this section by one plus the cumulative percent change in the non-seasonally adjusted Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, measured from the baseline dates specified in paragraph (c), as applicable, as further described in paragraph (b) of this section, and shall be rounded in accordance with paragraph (d) of this section.
(b)
Frequency.
(1)
In general—biennial adjustments.
Except as otherwise provided in paragraph (b)(2), (b)(3), or (b)(4) of this section, the adjustments described in paragraph (a) of this section shall be effective on October 1 following each consecutive two-year period ending August 30, using the non-seasonally adjusted Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers as of August 30 of that year.
(2)
First adjustments after baseline dates.
(i) The first adjustment described in paragraph (a) of this section shall, with respect to the thresholds specified in paragraph (c)(1), be effective on October 1, 2027, and shall be made using one plus the cumulative percent change in the non-seasonally adjusted Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers through August 30, 2027.
(ii) The first adjustment described in paragraph (a) of this section shall, with respect to the thresholds specified in paragraph (c)(2), be effective on October 1, 2029, and shall be made using one plus the cumulative percent change in the non-seasonally adjusted Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers through August 30, 2029.
(3)
Periods of high inflation—annual adjustments.
If the cumulative percent change of the non-seasonally adjusted Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, measured over the 12-month period ending August 30 following the year in which the most recent adjustment was made exceeds 8 percent, then the dollar thresholds shall be adjusted in accordance with paragraph (a) of this section using the cumulative percent change of the non-seasonally adjusted Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, measured over the 12-month period ending August 30 with an effective date of October 1 following the year in which the most recent adjustment was made.
(4)
Periods of negative inflation—no adjustments.
Notwithstanding paragraph (b)(1) or (b)(2) of this section,

§ 360.9
Large-bank deposit insurance determination modernization.
(a)
Purpose and scope.
This section is intended to allow the FDIC as receiver to continue to utilize the deposit and other operations of a large insured depository institution (defined as a “covered institution”) following failure. It also is intended to permit the FDIC to fulfill its legal mandates regarding the resolution of failed insured depository institutions to provide liquidity to depositors promptly and reduce the FDIC's costs by preserving the franchise value of a failed institution.
(b)
Definitions.
(1) A
covered institution
means an insured depository institution which, based on items as defined in Reports of Condition and Income filed with the appropriate Federal banking agency, has at least $2 billion in deposits and at least either:
(i) 250,000 deposit accounts; or
(ii) $20 billion in total assets, regardless of the number of deposit accounts.
(2) A
larger covered institution
is a covered institution which, based on items as defined in its Reports of Condition and Income filed with the appropriate Federal banking agency, has at least $2 billion in deposits and two million or more deposit accounts.
(3)
Number of deposit accounts and total assets
are as defined in the instructions for the filing of Reports of Condition and Income, as applicable to the insured depository institution for determining whether it qualifies as a covered institution or as a larger covered institution.
Deposit
has the same meaning as provided under section 3(
l
) of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act (
12 U.S.C. 1813
(
l
)). A
dually payable deposit
means any liability held in a foreign office of a U.S. insured depository institution that (1) would be a deposit if carried on the books and records of the insured depository institution in the United
(
printed page 69658)
States and (2) is expressly payable in the United States. A
domestic deposit
means any deposit other than a dually payable deposit. A
domestic deposit account
means any account that holds a domestic deposit. A
foreign deposit
means any dually payable deposit together with any liability held in a foreign office of a U.S. insured depository institution that (1) would be a deposit if carried on the books and records of the insured depository institution in the United States and (2) is not expressly payable in the United States. A
foreign deposit account
means any account that holds a foreign deposit. A
deposit account
means all domestic deposit accounts and all foreign deposit accounts, collectively. An
international banking facility deposit
has the same meaning as provided under section 3(
l
)(5)(B) of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act (
12 U.S.C. 1813
(
l
)). A
demand deposit account, NOW account, money market deposit account, savings deposit account and time deposit account
are as defined in the instructions for the filing of Reports of Condition and Income.
(4)
Sweep account arrangements
consist of a deposit account linked to an interest-bearing investment vehicle whereby funds are swept to and from the deposit account according to prearranged rules, usually on a daily basis, where the sweep investment vehicle is not a deposit and is reflected on the books and records of the covered institution.
(5)
Automated credit account arrangements
consist of a deposit account into which funds are automatically credited from an interest-bearing investment vehicle where the funds in the interest-bearing investment vehicle were not invested by prearranged rules.
(6)
Non-covered institution
means an insured depository institution that does not meet the definition of a covered institution.
(7)
Provisional hold
means an effective restriction on access to some or all of a deposit or other liability account after the failure of an insured depository institution.
(8)
Account holder
means the person or entity who has opened a deposit account with a covered institution and with whom the covered institution has a direct legal and contractual relationship with respect to the deposit.
(9)
Deposit account records
has the same meaning as provided in § 330.1(e) of this chapter.
(10)
Transactional features
with respect to a deposit account means that the account holder or the beneficial owner of deposits can make a transfer from the deposit account to a party other than the account holder, beneficial owner of deposits, or the larger covered institution itself, by a method that may result in such transfer being reflected in the end-of-day ledger balance for such deposit account on a day that is later than the day that such transfer is initiated, even if initiated prior to the larger covered institution's normal cutoff time for such transaction. A deposit account also has transactional features if preauthorized or automatic instructions provide for transfer of deposits in the deposit account to another deposit account at the same institution, if such other deposit account itself has transactional features.
(c) * * *
(1) A covered institution shall have in place an automated process for implementing a provisional hold on domestic deposit accounts, foreign deposit accounts, sweep account arrangements, and automated credit account arrangements immediately following the determination of the close-of-business account balances, as defined in § 360.8(b)(3), at the failed covered institution.
(2) The system requirements under paragraph (c)(1) of this section must have the capability of placing the provisional holds prescribed under that provision no later than 9 a.m. local time the day following the FDIC cutoff point, as defined in § 360.8(b)(1).

(4) For domestic deposit accounts, the provisional hold algorithm must be designed to exempt accounts below a specific account balance threshold, as determined by the FDIC. * * *

(5) For foreign deposit accounts, other than those connected to a sweep account arrangement or automated credit account arrangement, the provisional hold algorithm will apply a provisional hold percentage to the entire account balance. For foreign deposit accounts the provisional hold percentage may differ from that applied to domestic deposit accounts. Also, the provisional hold percentage would not vary by account category (
i.e.,
consumer versus non-consumer and transaction versus non-transaction) as is the case with domestic deposit accounts.
(6) For international banking facility deposits, other than those connected to a sweep account arrangement or automated credit account arrangement, the provisional hold algorithm will apply a provisional hold percentage to the entire account balance. For international banking facility deposits the provisional hold percentage may differ from that applied to domestic deposit accounts or foreign deposit accounts. Also, the provisional hold percentage would not vary by account category (
i.e.,
consumer versus non-consumer, and transaction versus non-transaction) as is the case with domestic deposit accounts.
(7) For the interest-bearing investment vehicle of a sweep account arrangement, the provisional hold algorithm must be designed with the capability to place a provisional hold on the interest-bearing investment vehicle with possibly a different account balance threshold and a different hold percentage according to the type of interest-bearing investment vehicle.

(d) * * *
(1)(i) A covered institution must have in place practices and procedures for providing the FDIC in a standard format upon the close of any day's business with required depositor and customer data for all deposit accounts held in domestic and foreign offices and interest-bearing investment accounts connected with sweep and automated credit account arrangements. Such standard data files are to be created through a mapping of pre-existing data elements and internal institution codes into standard data formats. Deposit account and customer data provided must be current as of the close of business for that day. Except as provided in paragraph (d)(1)(ii) of this section, a covered institution is not required to collect or generate depositor or customer data needed for deposit insurance calculation purposes that it does not ordinarily maintain in its records but must provide the data that it does maintain in its deposit account records in the required file format. A covered institution that is not a larger covered institution is not required to populate the outstanding debt flag or security pledge flag fields in lines 49 or 50 of appendix C to this part, even if the covered institution ordinarily maintains such records.
(ii) A larger covered institution must populate the mandatory data fields as indicated in appendices C through G to this part. If the larger covered institution does not have the required depositor and customer data needed to populate the mandatory data fields, then the larger covered institution must collect and maintain such data in its deposit account records for each account.
(iii) Notwithstanding the requirement set forth in paragraph (d)(1)(ii) of this section, a larger covered institution need not collect additional depositor and customer data and may, for

(A) For each deposit account for which a larger covered institution's deposit account records disclose the existence of a relationship which might provide a basis for additional deposit insurance in accordance with

(B) For each formal revocable trust account and each irrevocable trust account that is insured as described in

and for each irrevocable trust account that is insured as described in

(2) The requirements of paragraphs (d)(1)(i) through (iii) of this section shall be provided in five separate files, as indicated in appendices C through G to this part.
(3) Upon request by the FDIC, a covered institution must submit the data required by paragraphs (d)(1)(i) through (iii) of this section to the FDIC, in a manner prescribed by the FDIC.
(4) In providing the data required under paragraphs (d)(1)(i) through (iii) of this section to the FDIC, the covered institution must be able to reconcile the total deposit balances and the number of deposit accounts to the institution's subsidiary system control totals.
(5)(i) For each deposit account with transactional features for which a larger covered institution maintains its deposit account records as provided for under paragraph (d)(1)(iii) of this section, the larger covered institution must take steps reasonably calculated to ensure that the account holder will promptly provide to the FDIC the information needed for the FDIC to calculate deposit insurance with respect to each of those accounts. At a minimum, “steps reasonably calculated” shall include:
(A) A good faith effort to enter into contractual arrangements with the account holder that obligate the account holder to deliver information needed for deposit insurance calculation to the FDIC in a format prescribed in appendix I to this part within 24 hours after the appointment of the FDIC as receiver in order for the account holder to have access to deposits on the next business day after failure; or
(B) Providing the account holder with a written disclosure stating that, if the larger covered institution fails and the FDIC is appointed as receiver, then the account holder may not have access to deposits before delivery of information in a format prescribed in appendix I to this part.
(ii) A larger covered institution need not take the steps required pursuant to paragraph (d)(5)(i) of this section with respect to:
(A) Accounts maintained by a mortgage servicer, in a custodial or other fiduciary capacity, which are comprised of payments by mortgagors;
(B) Accounts maintained by real estate brokers, real estate agents, or title companies in which funds from multiple clients are deposited and held for a short period of time in connection with a real estate transaction;
(C) Accounts established by an attorney or law firm as Interest on Lawyers Trust Accounts, or functionally equivalent accounts;
(D) Accounts held in connection with an employee benefit plan (as defined in
12 CFR 330.14
); and
(E) An account maintained by an account holder for the benefit of others, to the extent that the deposits in the account are held for the benefit of:
(
1

12 CFR 330.10
; or
(
2

12 CFR 330.12
