(6) A larger covered institution may submit a request to the FDIC, using the address indicated in paragraph (g) of this section, for an exemption from the requirements of paragraph (d)(1) of this section for a relatively small number of accounts if circumstances exist that would make it impracticable or overly burdensome to meet those requirements with respect to certain types of accounts. Such requests may be in the form of a letter and must include a justification for the request and address the relative impact on customers' access to deposits in the event of failure. The FDIC will consider such requests on a case-by-case basis in light of the objectives of this section.
(e)
Implementation requirements.
(1) An insured depository institution that is a covered institution but not a larger covered institution as of [EFFECTIVE DATE OF THE FINAL RULE] must be in compliance with the requirements of this section as of [EFFECTIVE DATE OF THE FINAL RULE]. An insured depository institution that is a covered institution and a larger covered institution as of [EFFECTIVE DATE OF THE FINAL RULE] must comply with all the requirements of this section except the requirements under paragraph (c) of this section no later than [DATE 6 MONTHS AFTER THE EFFECTIVE DATE OF THE FINAL RULE] and the requirements of paragraph (c) of this section no later than [DATE 18 MONTHS AFTER THE EFFECTIVE DATE OF THE FINAL RULE]. Notwithstanding the prior two sentences, for any covered institution that became a covered institution before [EFFECTIVE DATE OF THE FINAL RULE] and has an initial compliance date that is after [EFFECTIVE DATE OF THE FINAL RULE], such institution must be in compliance with the requirements of this section no later than the relevant initial compliance date.
(2)(i) An insured depository institution not within the definition of a covered institution on [EFFECTIVE DATE OF THE FINAL RULE] must comply with the requirements of this section no later than eighteen months following the end of the second calendar quarter for which it meets the criteria for a covered institution.
(ii) Except as provided in paragraph (e)(4) or (5) of this section, an insured depository institution that is a covered institution but not a larger covered institution on [EFFECTIVE DATE OF THE FINAL RULE] must comply with the requirements set forth in paragraphs (d)(1)(ii) and (iii) and (d)(5) of this section no later than twelve months following the end of the second calendar quarter for which it meets the criteria for a larger covered institution.

Appendix I to Part 360—Pass-through and Broker Deposit Data Structure
This is the structure for the data file to provide passthrough deposit insurance data to the FDIC. Third parties would need to provide this data only in the event of a larger covered institution's failure. This data will facilitate the timely payment of funds. If data or information are not maintained or do not
(
printed page 69683)
apply, a null value in the appropriate field should be indicated. The file will be in a tab- or pipe-delimited ASCII format. Each file name will contain the third party's name or common abbreviation and the date of the extract. The files will be encrypted using an FDIC-supplied algorithm. The FDIC will transmit to the covered institution the encryption algorithm over FDIC
connect.
This data file will have one or more records for each deposit account at the bank, depending on the number of broker customers assigned to each account. Therefore, multiple records may have the same Bank_Acct_Identifier. Furthermore, if an account held by customers at the broker is owned by more than one person, multiple records could contain the same Bank_Acct_Identifier and Customer_Account_Number; these records would be differentiated by the Customer_Tax_ID and various Name fields. This file could also contain other records associated with the broker customer accounts to designate, among other things, beneficiaries, custodians, trustees, and agents as identified in field 30. This methodology allows the FDIC to know all the possible relationships for an individual account and whether a single customer is involved in many accounts.

[Release No. 34-106789; File Nos. S7-2026-07 and S7-2026-11]
(
printed page 69578)
October 30, 2026.
I. Introduction
A. Background
On December 13, 2023, the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission” or “SEC”) adopted amendments to Rule 17a9(a) and (e)(18)(iv)(A) and (B) under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Exchange Act”).
[
1
]
Under these amendments, covered clearing agencies that provide central counterparty services for U.S. Treasury securities (“U.S. Treasury securities CCAs”) must establish, implement, maintain, and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to establish objective, risk-based, and publicly disclosed criteria for participation which require that any direct participant of a U.S. Treasury securities CCA submit for clearance and settlement all of the eligible secondary market transactions to which such direct participant is a counterparty, and identify and monitor the U.S. Treasury securities CCA's direct participants' submission of transactions for clearing as required under the amendments (together, the “Trade Submission Requirement”).
[
2
]
The amendments defined what constitutes an “eligible secondary market transaction” to include, among other things, a secondary market transaction in U.S. Treasury securities of a type accepted for clearing by a registered covered clearing agency that is a repurchase or reverse repurchase agreement collateralized by U.S. Treasury securities (“repo transactions”), in which one of the counterparties is a direct participant of a covered clearing agency.
[
3
]
The amendments also included an exclusion from the definition of an eligible secondary market transaction for any repo transactions entered into between a direct participant and an affiliated counterparty (the “Inter-Affiliate Exclusion”), provided that the affiliated counterparty submit for clearance and settlement all other repo transactions to which the affiliate is a party (the “outward facing condition”).
[
4
]
The amendments define “affiliated counterparty” as any counterparty which meets the following criteria: (i) the counterparty is either a bank (as defined in
15 U.S.C. 78c(6)
), broker (as defined in
15 U.S.C. 78c(4)
), dealer (as defined in
15 U.S.C. 78c(5)
), or futures commission merchant (as defined in
7 U.S.C. 1a(28)
), or any entity regulated as a bank, broker, dealer, or futures commission merchant in its home jurisdiction; (ii) the counterparty holds, directly or indirectly, a majority ownership interest in the direct participant, or the direct participant, directly or indirectly, holds a majority ownership interest in the counterparty, or a third party, directly or indirectly, holds a majority ownership interest in both the direct participant and the counterparty; and (iii) the counterparty, direct participant, or third party referenced in paragraph (ii) of this definition as holding the majority ownership interest would be required to report its financial statements on a consolidated basis under U.S. Generally Accepted Accounting Principles or International Financial Reporting Standards, and such consolidated financial statements include the financial results of the majority-owned party or of both majority-owned parties.
[
5
]
B. IIB's and SIFMA's Requests for Exemptive Relief
The Commission has received requests for exemptive relief related to transactions by non-U.S. persons and related to the Inter-Affiliate Exclusion.
On February 27, 2026, the Institute of International Bankers (“IIB”) submitted a letter to the Commission requesting exemptive relief from the Trade Submission Requirement for certain non-U.S. transactions, specifically, the transactions of foreign financial institutions who are direct participants of a U.S. Treasury securities CCA when transacting with non-U.S. clients.
[
6
]
IIB explained that exemptive relief was appropriate because of legal uncertainty in certain foreign jurisdictions regarding the enforceability of fundamental clearing requirements, potential registration requirements for clearing firms operating in those jurisdictions, and practical concerns about repo transactions occurring when no U.S. Treasury securities CCA is operating.
[
7
]
On March 6, 2026, the Commission published the notice and encouraged interested persons to comment on the request for exemptive relief pursuant to Section 36 of the Exchange Act.
[
8
]
The initial comment period for the IIB Notice closed on April 10, 2026, and the Commission then reopened the comment period, which then closed on May 29, 2026.
[
9
]
On April 10, 2026, the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association (“SIFMA”) submitted a letter to the Commission requesting exemptive relief in two areas related to the Trade Submission Requirement.
[
10
]
First, SIFMA requested exemptive relief to expand the list of permitted affiliates with whom direct participants of a U.S. Treasury securities CCA could transact and rely upon the Inter-Affiliate Exclusion beyond the current set (
i.e.,
banks, broker-dealers, futures commission merchants, and their foreign equivalents) (the “SIFMA First Request”). Specifically, SIFMA requested that the Commission exercise its exemptive authority to allow a firm to treat all counterparties that meet clauses (ii) and (iii) of the definition in Rule 17ad-22(a) as affiliated counterparties, except for an affiliate that is an “investment company” as defined in Section 3 of the Investment Company Act of 1940 (regardless of whether such investment company is registered or required to be registered under that act).
[
11
]
Second, SIFMA requested that the outward-facing condition not include repo transactions between non-U.S.
(
printed page 69579)
affiliates and non-U.S. counterparties, to the extent that the direct participant does not exceed a specific activity level percentage threshold for those transactions (the “SIFMA Second Request”).
[
12
]
SIFMA explained that such relief was appropriate because non-U.S. affiliates commonly enter into transactions with each other for treasury, liquidity, and collateral management purposes that would raise serious logistical and cost concerns under the adopted rule.
[
13
]
On April 17, 2026, the Commission published the notice and encouraged interested persons to comment on the request for exemptive relief pursuant to Section 36 of the Exchange Act.
[
14
]
The comment period closed on May 29, 2026.
The Commission received certain comments on both Notices that suggested different approaches or modifications to the requested exempted relief.
[
15
]
In particular, certain commenters suggested that a unified or holistic approach to the issues presented in the IIB Notice and in the SIFMA Second Request may be workable, by incorporating elements from each Notice into one exemption, thus allowing for one exemption to generally address the issues raised in both Notices.
[
16
]
In response, on August 7, 2026, the Commission reopened the comment periods on both Notices, presenting a preliminary example of a unified approach and seeking additional feedback on certain targeted questions about the approach and alternative exemptive relief.
[
17
]
Both comment periods closed on August 31, 2026, and the Commission received additional comments on the issues raised in the Second Reopening Release.
[
18
]
II. Exemptive Relief for Qualifying Non-U.S. Transactions
A. Scope of Conditional Exemptive Relief
After considering the requests and the comments received on the IIB Notice, SIFMA's Second Request, and the Second Reopening Release, the Commission is issuing a conditional exemption, pursuant to Sections 36(a) and 17A(b)(1) of the Exchange Act, from the definition of an eligible secondary market transaction in Rule 17ad-22(a). Specifically, this exemption would exclude, from the definition of eligible secondary market transaction, a certain amount of a firm's
[
19
]
Qualifying Non-U.S. Transactions, as that term is defined below, provided that the two conditions set forth below are met.
First condition:
Either:
The quotient of the following is less than a specified percentage (“Percentage Cap”):
The market value
[
20
]
of the firm's Qualifying Non-U.S. Transactions; divided by
The sum of the market value of (i) all of the firm's cleared repo transactions, excluding such repo transactions entered into between a direct participant and an affiliated counterparty
[
21
]
(as discussed further below), and (ii) the firm's Qualifying Non-U.S. Transactions (
i.e.,
the numerator transactions) (collectively, the “Firm-Specific Threshold”);
Or:
The market value of the firm's Qualifying Non-U.S. Transactions are less than $5,000,000,000 (“Fixed Dollar Threshold”).
For purposes of this conditional exemption, “Qualifying Non-U.S. Transactions” means uncleared eligible secondary market transactions that are repo transactions between:
1. A “Non-U.S. Client”, meaning an entity that is not:
a. A direct participant of a U.S. Treasury securities CCA,
b. A U.S. person,
[
22
]
c. A U.S. branch of a non-U.S. person, or
d. A non-U.S. person whose obligations under the transaction are guaranteed by a U.S. person; and
2. An entity that is any of the following:
a. A “Non-U.S. Participant”, meaning a direct participant of a U.S. Treasury securities CCA that is not:
i. A U.S. person,
ii. A U.S. branch of a non-U.S. person;
iii. A non-U.S. person whose obligations under the transaction are guaranteed by a U.S. person; or
b. Any affiliated counterparty
[
23
]
of a direct participant of a U.S. Treasury securities CCA that is not:
i. A U.S. person,
ii. A U.S. branch of a non-U.S. person,
iii. A non-U.S. person whose obligations under the transaction are guaranteed by a U.S. person, or
c. A foreign branch
[
24
]
of a direct participant of a U.S. Treasury securities CCA that is a U.S. person.
Both the Firm-Specific Threshold and Fixed Dollar Threshold would be calculated using a rolling daily average of the immediately prior three quarters as the “Assessment Period,” with each quarter being weighted equally.
[
25
]
The Percentage Cap would initially be 25% and would decrease over time, as follows:
(
printed page 69580)
Applicable
                             percentage cap
Time period
25
June 30, 2027 through June 30, 2028.
20
July 1, 2028 through June 30, 2029.
15
July 1, 2029 through June 30, 2030.
10
After June 30, 2030.
Second condition:
A direct participant of a U.S. Treasury securities CCA attests to any U.S. Treasury securities CCA of which it is a direct participant that such direct participant is monitoring and complying with the terms of the first condition set forth above. In the event a direct participant does not satisfy the first condition, it immediately notifies any U.S. Treasury securities CCA of which it is a direct participant and informs each such CCA of its plan for returning to compliance with the conditional exemptive relief, or that it will no longer avail itself of the conditional exemptive relief. Each such U.S. Treasury securities CCA will then be able to determine any appropriate action on its part, consistent with the CCA's rules.
The Firm-Specific Threshold is based on suggestions from IIB
[
26
]
and on SIFMA's Second Request, which contains a percentage cap,
[
27
]
a numerator consisting of transactions that were exempted from the Trade Submission Requirement,
[
28
]
and a denominator consisting of a measure of the firm's total repo transaction activity added to the transactions in the numerator.
[
29
]
The Commission has modified the scope of the Firm-Specific Threshold to encompass the relief requested in the IIB Notice and in response to suggestions from commenters,
[
30
]
including those that commented on a preliminary version of this Firm-Specific Threshold in the Second Reopening Release.
[
31
]
The Commission made several changes from the preliminary version of this Firm-Specific Threshold presented in the Second Reopening Release. In response to commenters, the denominator now excludes “such repo transactions entered into between a direct participant and an affiliated counterparty,” as commenters stated that such transactions were not market transactions and should not be included as a measure of the firm's market activity.
[
32
]
Recognizing that certain corporate entities may have multiple direct participants, the Commission has also clarified that “firm,” as it relates to the first condition, applies to any direct participant of a U.S. Treasury securities CCA, together with its affiliates, which would include other direct participants.
[
33
]
The Commission has also revised the denominator to consist of the firm's cleared repo transactions.
[
34
]
This revision allows the firm's denominator to include cleared repo transactions that are not eligible secondary market transactions, because they are excluded from that definition because of the counterparty.
[
35
]
This change therefore incentivizes a firm to clear certain repo transactions, even when not required.
[
36
]
The Firm-Specific Threshold is subject to a Percentage Cap that falls over time, from 25% initially and for the first year, to 20% for the second year, 15% for the third year, and ending at 10% after June 30, 2030. Several commenters suggested various approaches for percentage caps.
[
37
]
The Commission believes this phased approach with a final Percentage Cap of 10% most appropriately balances the need for the exemption to be narrow while also recognizing that market participants, particularly foreign entities, may need time to change or adapt business practices, onboard clients, obtain legal opinions, or update systems in order to comply.
[
38
]
The Commission has also added the Fixed Dollar Threshold to the conditional exemptive relief. The idea of exemptive relief that was not derived from a firm's cleared repo transactions was first suggested by commenters to level the playing field between market participants with a large U.S. domestic Treasury repo business and market participants with smaller volume Treasury repo businesses that are more heavily focused outside the U.S.
[
39
]
As first suggested, such a threshold would have been calculated by dividing market-wide transaction activity in Treasury repo by a measure of direct participants at a U.S. Treasury securities CCA.
[
40
]
The Commission solicited comments about whether such a threshold was necessary and how it should be calculated in the Second Reopening Release.
[
41
]
In response, one commenter reemphasized the importance of such a threshold but, acknowledging potential difficulties with its calculation as initially suggested, proposed a fixed dollar amount threshold of $10 billion to account for future growth in U.S. Treasury repo activity.
[
42
]
Another commenter was not opposed to a fixed dollar amount threshold but cautioned the Commission to avoid setting the threshold so high that it would create a bifurcated market.
[
43
]
The Commission is setting the threshold at $5 billion, based
(
printed page 69581)
on its current understanding of the U.S. Treasury market, to accommodate the need for such a threshold while reducing the risk of a bifurcated market. The Commission will monitor the Fixed Dollar Threshold going forward to consider whether it remains appropriately tailored to the U.S. Treasury market.
The Commission has also added a second condition to the exemptive relief to ensure that the U.S. Treasury securities CCAs that are tasked with enforcing the Trade Submission Requirement are provided information to allow them to better understand whether their direct participants are relying on this exemption and to ensure that those direct participants affirm that they are monitoring and complying with the conditional relief herein.
B. Discussion of the Conditional Exemptive Relief for Qualifying Non-U.S. Transactions
Section 36(a) of the Exchange Act authorizes the Commission, by rule, regulation or order, to exempt, either conditionally or unconditionally, any person, security or transaction, or any class or classes of persons, securities, or transactions, from any provision or provisions of the Exchange Act or any rule or regulation thereunder, to the extent that such exemption is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, and is consistent with the protection of investors.
[
44
]
In addition, under Section 17A(b)(1) of the Exchange Act, the Commission, by rule or order, upon its own motion or upon application, may conditionally or unconditionally exempt any clearing agency or security or any class of clearing agencies or securities from any provisions of this section or the rules or regulations thereunder, if the Commission finds that such exemption is consistent with the public interest, the protection of investors, and the purposes of this section, including the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions and the safeguarding of securities and funds.
[
45
]
For the reasons discussed below, the Commission is using its authority under Section 36 and Section 17A of the Exchange Act to provide a conditional exemption from the definition of an eligible secondary market transaction under Rule 17ad-22(a), meaning that a U.S. Treasury securities CCA will be exempt from enforcing the Trade Submission Requirement with respect to Qualifying Non-U.S. Transactions if the conditions stated above are met. The Commission finds such conditional exemption to be necessary or appropriate in the public interest and consistent with the protection of investors, as required under Section 36, and with the purposes of Section 17A of the Exchange Act, including the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions and the safeguarding of securities and funds, as required under Section 17A.
First, the conditional exemption would allow financial institutions to better accommodate repo transactions within an affiliated group involving non-U.S. affiliates for purposes of treasury, liquidity, and collateral management. As the Commission stated in the Adopting Release, inter-affiliate transactions represent an important tool to transfer liquidity and risk within an affiliated group.
[
46
]
These transactions may serve different purposes, including, but not limited to, providing U.S. Treasury securities for delivery when an affiliate has taken a long or short position in U.S. Treasury securities as a hedge against other exposures, allowing the movement of U.S. Treasury securities to allow them to be posted as margin on an affiliate's transaction, ensuring that U.S. Treasury securities can serve as a liquidity buffer for an affiliated bank, or to meet liquidity composition targets.
[
47
]
To get the U.S. Treasury securities to the appropriate entity within an affiliated group, the affiliate often enters into repos or reverse repos with a direct participant of a U.S. Treasury securities CCA.
[
48
]
Market participants have explained that, as adopted, the terms of the Inter-Affiliate Exclusion effectively negate its utility, because in order to use the exclusion, an affiliate must centrally clear all outward-facing repos pursuant to the outward-facing condition.
[
49
]
As a result, market participants have claimed that two non-U.S. affiliates of a direct participant would be required to clear a repo transaction between themselves if either affiliate enters into an uncleared repo transaction with a direct participant, raising costs and burdens for an activity commonly used between non-U.S. affiliates for treasury, liquidity, and collateral management activities.
[
50
]
The Commission agrees with these market participants that this restriction on transactions between non-U.S. affiliates could have destabilizing effects, such as limiting the ability for a non-U.S. affiliate to obtain funding through a repo transaction with another non-U.S. affiliate when U.S. Treasury securities CCAs are closed.
[
51
]
Because of this exemption, non-U.S. affiliates of a direct participant will be able to use inter-affiliate transactions for treasury, liquidity, and collateral management with each other, subject to the specified conditions. This exemptive relief should help ensure that non-U.S. affiliates are not forced to clear internal treasury, liquidity, or collateral transactions with the direct participant (which, if required, would eliminate the practical value of the Inter-Affiliate Exclusion) or reduce their participation in U.S. Treasury repo activity with non-U.S. counterparties. The Commission believes that the scope of this exemption, including the Percentage Cap and the Fixed Dollar Threshold, ensures that it applies in limited circumstances, meaning that the benefits of increased central clearing identified in the Adopting Release will still be present.
[
52
]
Therefore, the exemption is consistent with promoting the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions, the public interest, and the protection of investors.
Second, the conditional exemption should allow foreign financial institutions that are direct participants of U.S. Treasury securities CCAs and U.S. financial institutions that have foreign branches or affiliates to accommodate transactions with Non-U.S. Clients. Without such an exemption, such transactions may face legal uncertainty regarding certain aspects of central clearing, such as the enforceability of netting contracts in relevant jurisdictions (including close-out netting in a default scenario), and operational challenges due to, for example, time zones and transactions occurring when no U.S. Treasury securities CCA is open.
[
53
]
Further, the Commission understands that, as a practical matter, many non-U.S.
(
printed page 69582)
counterparties do not engage in U.S. Treasury repo activity at a level that makes onboarding to a U.S. Treasury securities CCA economically or operationally feasible.
[
54
]
This conditional exemptive relief allows for direct participants of U.S. Treasury securities CCAs to continue to transact with such non-U.S. counterparties without having to incur overly burdensome costs for a relatively limited amount of transactions, while ensuring, through the narrow terms of the exemption, that the amount of transactions being centrally cleared and risk managed continues to increase. Thus, the exemption is consistent with reducing the contagion risk to a U.S. Treasury securities CCA,
[
55
]
which in turn, is consistent with promoting the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of U.S. Treasury securities and the safeguarding of securities and funds.
Third, issuing one conditional exemption to address concerns related to both non-U.S. transactions and the Inter-Affiliate Exclusion should facilitate administration of the relief sought with respect to such transactions (meaning, it should be more efficient for market participants to manage compliance with one holistic exemption, as opposed to two very similar exemptions that have to be calculated separately).
[
56
]
Market participants could manage and build reporting systems based on one set of conditions, as opposed to two, thereby decreasing burden and potential operational costs of set-up and ongoing compliance. Such an approach is therefore consistent with promoting the public interest.
Fourth, the condition regarding attestation to any U.S. Treasury securities CCA of which a firm is a direct participant should help ensure that such CCAs can better understand whether their direct participants are relying upon this exemption and, as necessary, seek additional information from direct participants that would allow such CCAs to consider how direct participants are complying with such CCAs' rules pursuant to the Trade Submission Requirement.
[
57
]
Facilitating the ability of a U.S. Treasury securities CCA to understand its direct participants' activity, and therefore also facilitating the ability to enforce the Trade Submission Requirement, is consistent with promoting the public interest.
Finally, phasing in reductions to the Percentage Cap over a period of three years should ensure that market participants have sufficient time to arrange compliance with the conditions of the exemptive relief by initially allowing a greater percentage of Qualifying Non-U.S. Transactions to qualify under the exemption while gradually reducing that percentage.
[
58
]
The Commission recognizes that market participants may need to change or adapt certain business practices to ensure compliance with the exemption, and phasing in reductions to the Percentage Cap should allow market participants time to take any necessary steps to comply with the Trade Submission Requirement and the conditional exemption issued herein, such as onboarding clients, obtaining legal opinions, or updating systems accordingly. Therefore, reducing the Percentage Cap over time allows market participants time to adapt or change business practices over several years, as opposed to all at once, which should allow for smoother implementation for the U.S. Treasury market, which is therefore in the public interest and consistent with the protection of investors.
III. Exemptive Relief for Affiliated Counterparties
A. Scope of Exemptive Relief
As discussed above, the SIFMA First Request asked the Commission to provide exemptive relief to treat all counterparties that meet clauses (ii) and (iii) of the definition in Rule 17ad-22(a) as affiliated counterparties, except for an affiliate that is an investment company.
Rule 17ad-22(a) defines an affiliated counterparty as any counterparty which meets the following criteria: (i) The counterparty is either a bank (as defined in
15 U.S.C. 78c(6)
), broker (as defined in
15 U.S.C. 78c(4)
), dealer (as defined in
15 U.S.C. 78c(5)
), or futures commission merchant (as defined in
7 U.S.C. 1a(28)
), or any entity regulated as a bank, broker, dealer, or futures commission merchant in its home jurisdiction; (ii) The counterparty holds, directly or indirectly, a majority ownership interest in the direct participant, or the direct participant, directly or indirectly, holds a majority ownership interest in the counterparty, or a third party, directly or indirectly, holds a majority ownership interest in both the direct participant and the counterparty; and (iii) The counterparty, direct participant, or third party referenced in paragraph (ii) of this definition as holding the majority ownership interest would be required to report its financial statements on a consolidated basis under U.S. Generally Accepted Accounting Principles or International Financial Reporting Standards, and such consolidated financial statements include the financial results of the majority-owned party or of both majority-owned parties.
[
59
]
After considering the SIFMA First Request and the comments received upon the request, the Commission is providing an exemption, pursuant to Sections 36(a) and 17A(b)(1) of the Exchange Act, from the definition of an eligible secondary market transaction in Rule 17ad-22(a). Specifically, this exemption would exclude, from the definition of eligible secondary market transaction, repo transactions between a direct participant of a U.S. Treasury securities CCA and any entity that meets the criteria in parts (ii) and (iii) of the definition of an affiliated counterparty in Rule 17ad-22(a), provided that the entity is not an “investment company” as defined in Section 3 of the Investment Company Act of 1940 (regardless of whether such investment company is registered or required to be registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940).
[
60
]
(
printed page 69583)
B. Discussion of Exemptive Relief for Affiliated Counterparties
Section 36(a) of the Exchange Act authorizes the Commission, by rule, regulation or order, to exempt, either conditionally or unconditionally, any person, security or transaction, or any class or classes of persons, securities, or transactions, from any provision or provisions of the Exchange Act or any rule or regulation thereunder, to the extent that such exemption is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, and is consistent with the protection of investors. In addition, under Section 17A(b)(1) of the Exchange Act, the Commission, by rule or order, upon its own motion or upon application, may conditionally or unconditionally exempt any clearing agency or security or any class of clearing agencies or securities from any provisions of this section or the rules or regulations thereunder, if the Commission finds that such exemption is consistent with the public interest, the protection of investors, and the purposes of this section, including the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions and the safeguarding of securities and funds.
For the reasons discussed below, the Commission finds this exemption necessary or appropriate in the public interest and consistent with the protection of investors, as required under Section 36, and with the purposes of Section 17A of the Exchange Act, including the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions and the safeguarding of securities and funds, as required under Section 17A.
Commenters have explained that many affiliates of direct participants rely on repo transactions with that direct participant for purposes of liquidity, treasury, and collateral management. Many such affiliates are not banks, broker-dealers, or futures commission merchants, and are thus ineligible for the Inter-Affiliate Exclusion as adopted. Thus, absent this exemptive relief, these transactions between a non-bank/broker-dealer/futures commission merchant affiliate and the direct participant would be required to be cleared, even if the affiliate does not conduct any external customer-facing activity or subject the direct participant to any external risk.
[
61
]
According to commenters, such a requirement would impose serious costs and delays, consume balance sheet and clearing capacity, and increase risks to non-U.S. affiliates (and their customers) with liquidity and collateral needs during the hours in which no U.S. Treasury CCA is operating.
[
62
]
Therefore, by allowing direct participants to utilize the Inter-Affiliate Exclusion for transactions with a broader array of affiliates, the exemption should better accommodate transactions within an affiliated group involving non-U.S. affiliates or foreign branches for purposes of treasury, liquidity, and collateral management. This will lower costs and reduce delays by not requiring the unnecessary clearing of inter-affiliate transactions when an affiliate that is not a bank, broker-dealer, or futures commission merchant enters into an inter-affiliate transaction with a direct participant. At the same time, the exemption does not apply to inter-affiliate transactions between a direct participant and an affiliate that is an “investment company” under the Investment Company Act of 1940, because such an affiliate may pose additional risk to the direct participant due to it taking market positions on the value of securities.
[
63
]
IV. Conclusion
Accordingly,
It is ordered,
pursuant to Sections 17A and 36 of the Exchange Act, that the Commission grants a conditional exemption for the transactions described in Part II of this Order, from the definition of an eligible secondary market transaction in Rule 17ad-22(a), and an exemption as described in Part III of this Order from the definition of an eligible secondary market transaction in Rule 17ad-22(a).

Department of Homeland Security
[Docket No. CISA-2026-0199]
AGENCY:
Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Department of Homeland Security (DHS).
ACTION:
30-Day notice of information collection; request for comment; extension of previously approved collection 1670-0013.
SUMMARY:
The Office of the Chief Security Officer (OCSO) within Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) submits the following information collection request (ICR) to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review and clearance. CISA previously published this information collection request (ICR) in the
Federal Register
on September 10, 2026 for a 60-day public comment period. No comments were received by CISA. The purpose of this notice is to allow additional 30-days for public comments.
DATES:
Comments are encouraged and will be accepted until December 4, 2026. Submissions received after the deadline for receiving comments may not be considered.
ADDRESSES:
Written comments and recommendations for the proposed information collection should be sent within 30 days of publication of this notice to
www.reginfo.gov/​public/​do/​PRAMain

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Partnerships between the U.S. Government and the state, local tribal and private sector at times necessitate the sharing of classified information. The State, Local, Tribal and Private Sector (SLTPS) Clearance Request Form facilitates this sharing by sponsoring security clearances for certain members of each sector based on either their membership on a Sector Coordinating Council (SCC)/association or their infrastructure protection job-related duties and their need-to-know. The SLTPS is designed to sponsor security clearances for state, local, tribal and private sector officials involved in the infrastructure protection mission. These partners are subject matter experts within specific industries and have specialized knowledge not available within the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and other Federal Departments or Agencies. Private citizens do not receive monetary compensation for their time. CISA created this program to sponsor clearances for these individuals who are not employed by or contracted with another Federal agency (the traditional means of obtaining a clearance) and must have clearances.
CISA collects necessary information through 1670-0013 to facilitate security clearances needed for sharing classified information with the vetted SLTPS Stakeholders.
The U.S. Government is authorized to ask for this information under Sections 201 and 229 of the Homeland Security Act (
Pub. L. 107-296
,
6 U.S.C. 121
,
150
), and Executive Orders 12968, 13526, 13549, 13636, and 13691 which authorize the collection of this information.
In order to begin this process of adjudicating a nominee to participate in the clearance program, federal nominators will complete the DHS Form 9014, State, Local, Tribal and Private Sector Clearance Request Form. The federal nominator will sign the form and have it approved by a senior-level official from the corresponding Federal Department or Agency. The signatures indicate the nominator and senior-level official have deemed the applicant has a CISA mission and meets the requirements and criteria as outlined in Executive Order (E.O.) 13549, the Department of Homeland Security, Classified National Security Information Program for SLTPS Implementing Directive and
E.O. 13691
, Sec. 4(c), and
32 CFR
, Part 117, Sec. 117.22 of the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM). Once submitted to the CISA OCSO the SLTPS Administrator will request the Personally Identifiable Information (PII) and a record is created into the Integrated Security Management System (ISMS). The Security Specialist will initiate an eApplication (eAPP), the
(
printed page 69570)
Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency secure portal for investigation processing. Once the data is entered into e-App, the nominee is provided a password and can access the system and complete the online security questionnaire.
This information is only available to Security Specialists within OCSO working on the program and is maintained in ISMS, which is “owned” by the OCSO. The two-part PII request process helps minimize the collection of sensitive PII for only those nominees who meet the threshold and are sponsored by CISA.
This is an extension of a previously approved information collection.

AGENCY:
Fish and Wildlife Service, Interior.
ACTION:
Notice of information collection; request for comment.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, we, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Service), are proposing to revise an existing information collection.
DATES:
Interested persons are invited to submit comments on or before December 4, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Written comments and recommendations for the proposed information collection should be sent within 30 days of publication of this notice to
https://www.reginfo.gov/​public/​do/​PRAMain
.
Find this particular information collection by selecting “Currently under Review—Open for Public Comments” or by using the search function. Please provide a copy of your comments to the Service Information Collection Clearance Officer, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, MS: PRB (JAO/3W), 5275 Leesburg Pike, Falls Church, VA 22041-3803 (mail); or by email to
Info_Coll@fws.gov
.
Please reference “1018-0186” in the subject line of your comments.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Madonna L. Baucum, Service Information Collection Clearance Officer, by email at
Info_Coll@fws.gov
,
or by telephone at (703) 358-2503. Individuals in the United States who are deaf, deafblind, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability may dial 711 (TTY, TDD, or TeleBraille) to access telecommunications relay services. Individuals outside the United States should use the relay services offered within their country to make international calls to the point-of-contact in the United States. You may also view the information collection request (ICR) at
https://www.reginfo.gov/​public/​do/​PRAMain
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA;
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
) and its implementing regulations in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) at
5 CFR part 1320
, all information collections require approval under the PRA. We may not conduct or sponsor, and you are not required to respond to, a collection of information unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number.
On June 8, 2026, we published in the
Federal Register
(
91 FR 34639
) a notice of our intent to request that OMB approve this information collection. In that notice, we solicited comments for 60 days, ending on August 7, 2026. We also published the
Federal Register
notice on
Regulations.gov
(Docket No. FWS-HQ-IA-2026-1948). We received the following six comments in response to that notice:
Comment 1:
Electronic comment received from Victoria Lopez submitted via
Regulations.gov
(FWS-HQ-IA-2026-1948-0003) on August 3, 2026. The commenter requests that the Service stop allowing the import of African elephants into the United States and stop authorizing the killing of elephants for trophies. The commenter expresses broader opposition to elephant hunting and trophy imports and raises concerns about threats to African elephant populations. The commenter also cites information regarding elephant populations and trophy hunting in Botswana and other African countries and urges the Service to provide greater protection for elephants and deny permits for the import of elephant trophies.
Agency Response to Comment 1:
The Service appreciates the commenter's concern for the conservation of African elephants. However, the comments regarding whether African elephants should be hunted, whether elephant hunting should be permitted in range countries, and whether the Service should issue permits for the import of elephant specimens are outside the scope of this information collection renewal. The commenter did not address the information collection requirements; therefore, no response is required.
Comment 2:
Anonymous electronic comment submitted via
Regulations.gov
[FWS-HQ-IA-2026-1948-0004] on August 5, 2026. The commenter states that they are unclear about the changes regarding elephant trophies and generally support sport hunting when conducted within biological limits established by range countries. The commenter opposes unnecessary burdens on hunting and indicates they take no position otherwise. The commenter also states that the action appears to primarily concern live elephants and expresses support for the Service's judgment.
Agency Response to Comment 2:
We appreciate the commenters support regarding the import of African elephant specimens and feel there are no unnecessary burdens on hunting. Therefore, the Service is taking no action in response to the comment.
Comment 3:
Anonymous electronic comment submitted via
Regulations.gov
[FWS-HQ-IA-2026-1948-0005] on August 7, 2026. The commenter recommends prohibiting the import and export of wildlife for hunting purposes and expresses concerns about climate change and the impacts of hunting on threatened species, including elephants.
Agency Response to Comment 3:
This renewal does not propose changes to the African elephant 4(d) rule, the conservation status of African elephants, or the Service's substantive
(
printed page 69571)
standards for authorizing the import of African elephant specimens. The commenter did not address the information collection requirements; therefore, no response is required.
Comment 4:
Anonymous electronic comment submitted via
Regulations.gov
[FWS-HQ-IA-2026-1948-0006] on August 7, 2026. The commenter asserts that the information collection does not have sufficient practical utility under the Paperwork Reduction Act because Form 3-200-37 may provide self-certified information concerning conservation benefits, population status, and facility suitability. The commenter recommends requiring third-party financial audits and peer-reviewed biological population data before OMB approves the information collection.
Agency Response to Comment 4:
The Service considers the information collected through Form 3-200-37 necessary and to have practical utility in administering the existing requirements. Therefore, the Service is taking no action in response to the comment.
Comment 5:
Electronic comment received from Allyson Koop, volunteer with Animal Counsel, submitted via
Regulations.gov
[FWS-HQ-IA-2026-1948-0007] on August 7, 2026. The commenter supports the existing information collection and recognizes its utility in evaluating applications. The commenter recommends requiring applicants to provide additional corroboration of proposed activities, such as a letter of reference, facility photographs, or a detailed care plan, to help the Service assess an applicant's ability to properly care for an African elephant. The commenter also supports electronic applications as a means of reducing applicant burden.
Agency Response to Comment 5:
The Service appreciates the commenter's support for the form and electronic application process. Their recommendation to require additional information modifying the current requirements would require a separate regulatory action that is currently outside the scope of this renewal request. However, the Service will take the recommendation under consideration should we pursue any additional regulatory actions regarding the requirements for African elephants.
Comment 6:
Electronic comment received from W. Laird Hamberlin, President, Safari Club International, submitted via
Regulations.gov
[FWS-HQ-IA-2026-1948-0008] on August 7, 2026. The commenter asserts that the 2024 African elephant 4(d) rule including its annual certification for African elephant range countries is unnecessary, duplicative, and overly burdensome, and recommends its elimination or amendment and that CITES requirements are sufficient.
Agency Response to Comment 6:
This renewal does not propose changes to the African elephant 4(d) rule, the conservation status of African elephants, or the Service's substantive standards for authorizing the import of African elephant specimens. Although the certification is part of the information collection, eliminating or modifying the requirement would require a separate regulatory action. The Service will take the recommendation under consideration should we pursue any additional regulatory actions regarding the requirements for African elephants.
As part of our continuing effort to reduce paperwork and respondent burdens, we are soliciting comments from the public and other Federal agencies on the proposed ICR described below. We are especially interested in public comments addressing the following:
(1) Whether or not the collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the agency, including whether or not the information will have practical utility;
(2) The accuracy of our estimate of the burden for this collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used;
(3) Ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and
(4) How might the agency minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are to respond, including through the use of appropriate automated, electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection techniques or other forms of information technology (
e.g.,
permitting electronic submission of response).
Comments that you submit in response to this notice are a matter of public record. Before including your address, phone number, email address, or other personally identifiable information in your comment, you should be aware that your entire comment—including your personally identifiable information—may be publicly available at any time. While you can ask us in your comment to withhold your personally identifiable information from public review, we cannot guarantee that we will be able to do so.
Abstract:
The general permit provisions in
50 CFR part 13
provide the uniform rules, conditions, and procedures for activities requiring a permit under all laws, treaties, and regulations administered by the Service. The requirements in
50 CFR part 13
are in addition to any other permit regulations that may apply to a specific circumstance.
When a species is listed as threatened, section 4(d) of the Endangered Species Act of 1973, as amended (ESA;
16 U.S.C. 1533
), gives discretion to the Secretary of the Interior (Secretary) to issue regulations that the Secretary deems necessary and advisable to provide for the conservation of such species. Considering the rise in international trade of live elephants, particularly of wild-sourced elephants, and recent CITES developments concerning regulation of trade in live elephants, as well as a need to clarify our enhancement standards and improve the permitting process for import of sport-hunted elephant trophies, we reevaluated the provisions of the regulations that were issued under section 4(d) of the ESA for the African elephant. We found it is appropriate for the U.S. to adopt requirements under the ESA to ensure that activities with live African elephants under U.S. jurisdiction enhance the conservation of the species and that live African elephants are well cared for, so that any domestic demand for live African elephants enhances their conservation and does not contribute to their decline in the wild.
In addition, clarifying the enhancement requirement for the import of African elephant sport-hunted trophies and receiving information from the range countries enables us to ensure that authorized imports contribute to enhancing the conservation of the species and do not contribute to the decline of the species. Clarifying the enhancement standards in the decision-making process for the import of African elephant sport-hunted trophies increases transparency with stakeholders. To support U.S. African elephant conservation efforts, we allow certain types of imports only from countries that have achieved a Category One (see information for category designations below) designation under the CITES National Legislation Project, which is accomplished by meeting the basic requirements to implement CITES through the Party's adoption of national laws to implement the treaty.
On April 1, 2024, we issued a rule (
89 FR 22522
) which revised regulations promulgated under ESA section 4(d) rule (
50 CFR 17.40(e)
) by adopting measures that were necessary and advisable for the current conservation needs of the species, based on our evaluation of the current threats to the African elephant. This final section 4(d) rule removed from
50 CFR 17.40(e)(2)
(
printed page 69572)
the exception from prohibitions for import, export, interstate commerce, and foreign commerce in live African elephants, except when a permit can be issued under
50 CFR part 17
. The final rule also established the standards used to evaluate “enhancement” under the ESA for the import of wild-sourced live African elephants under a new
50 CFR 17.40(e)(10)
. This provision established an annual certification requirement for range countries that allow for export of live African elephants destined for the United States to provide the Service with information about the management and status of African elephants in their country.
This final rule also clarified our evaluation of the existing enhancement requirement regarding applications for the import of sport-hunted trophies by adding a new provision to
50 CFR 17.40(e)(6)
. This provision established an annual certification requirement for range countries that allow for export of sport-hunted trophies destined for the United States to provide the Service with information about the management and status of African elephants and the hunting programs in their country. This provision did not change the enhancement requirement for the import of sport-hunted trophies under the previous section 4(d) rule but clarified how that requirement can be met.
The final rule also incorporated the CITES National Legislation Project category designations (see
50 CFR 23.7
and
https://www.cites.org
) into the acceptance of imports under
50 CFR 17.40(e)(2)
,
(e)(6)
, and
(e)(10)
under a new
50 CFR 17.40(e)(11)
.
Before a country can issue an export permit for CITES Appendix I or II specimens, the CITES Scientific Authority of the exporting country must determine that the export will not be detrimental to the species, and the Management Authority must be satisfied that the specimens were acquired legally. For the export of Appendix III specimens, the Management Authority must be satisfied that the specimens were acquired legally (CITES does not require findings from the Scientific Authority). Prior to the importation of Appendix I specimens, both the scientific and Management Authorities of the importing country must make required findings. The Scientific Authority must also monitor trade of all species to ensure that the level of trade is sustainable.
Article VIII(3) of the CITES treaty states that participating parties should make efforts to ensure that CITES specimens are traded with a minimum of delay. Section XII of Resolution Conf. 12.3 (Rev. CoP20)
Permits and certificates
recommends use of simplified procedures for issuing CITES documents to expedite trade that will have no impact, or a negligible impact on conservation of the species involved.
All Service permit applications use forms in the 3-200 series, with each form tailored to a specific activity and its corresponding permitting requirements. We collect standard identifier information for all permits, such as the name of the applicant and the applicant's address, telephone numbers, tax identification number, email address, and website address, if applicable. Standardization of general information common to the application forms makes filing applications easier for the public, as well as expediting our review of applications.
The information that we collect on applications and reports is the minimum necessary for us to determine if the applicant meets/continues to meet issuance requirements for the particular activity. Respondents submit application forms periodically as needed; submission of reports is generally on an annual basis, or as identified conditionally as part of an issued permit. We examined applications in this collection, focusing on questions frequently misinterpreted or not addressed by applicants. We have made clarifications to many of our applications to make it easier for the applicant to know what information we need and to accommodate future electronic permitting. Use of these forms:
Reduces burden on applicants.
Improves customer service.
Allows us to process applications and finalize reviews quickly.
We will request OMB approval to renew, without change, the reporting and recordkeeping requirements identified below:
(1) Permit Application (Form 3-200-37h), “
Interstate Commerce, Transfer, Export, or Foreign Commerce of Live African Elephants under the U.S. Endangered Species Act (ESA)”
50 CFR 17.40
—Form 3-200-37h will cover activities involving the interstate commerce, transfer, export, or foreign commerce of live African elephants. The application form applies to both wild-sourced and captive-bred live African elephants. The information provided in the application form will be used to determine whether a permit can be issued to the applicant under the relevant Federal regulations pertaining to the requested activity. We collect the following information from domestic entities (
i.e.,
individuals, private sector, State/local/Tribal governments), noting applicants may need to provide information from the foreign entity as part of their application submission:
Standardized identifier information required in
50 CFR 13.12
.
Name and address where the permit is to be mailed, if different from physical address.
Name, phone number, and email of individual(s) for the Service to contact with questions.
Whether the applicant or any owners of the business (if applying as a business, corporation, or institution) have been assessed a civil penalty or convicted of any criminal provision of any statute or regulation relating to the activity for which the application is filed; been convicted, or entered a plea of guilty or nolo contendere, for a felony violation of the Lacey Act, the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, or the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act; forfeited collateral; or are currently under charges for any violation of the laws.
Type of activity requested (interstate commerce, transfer, export, or foreign commerce).
The current location of the animal(s) (if different from the physical address).
Name and physical address of the recipient of the specimen.
For each animal involved in the export/transport, the applicant must provide the following information:
—Scientific name (genus, species, and if applicable, subspecies);
—Common name;
—Approximate birth date (mm/dd/yyyy);
—Wild or captive-bred;
—Quantity;
—Sex (males, females,
e.g.,
10.2); and
—Permanent markings or identification (microchip #, leg band #, tattoos, studbook #, etc.).
Information regarding source of specimen(s).
A description and justification for the requested activity.
Information regarding technical expertise and facilities.
Information confirming that the receiving facility meets the CITES “suitably equipped to house and care for” requirements.
The transportation/shipment condition of the live animals.
A.
Recordkeeping Requirements
—Completion of Form 3-200-37h requires the retention of records regarding details on the identification of the elephants, as well as regarding their acquisition, original source, and subsequent transfers, as well as records documenting staff technical expertise and facility information for the species.
(
printed page 69573)
B.
Permit Fee
—Form 3-200-37h imposes a nonhour burden cost of $100 per application. Amendments will incur a $50 processing fee.
(2) Range Country Certification Requirements—As described above, the final rule establishes an annual certification requirement for range countries to provide the Service with information about the management and status of African elephants and their habitat, within their country. This is not part of the application form itself, but rather a separate certification document/report/letter from the foreign country's government. The foreign government may provide the certification and information directly to the Service, or the applicant may provide it to the Service. The certification and information will be subject to verification by the Service.
This annual certification from the range country will be kept on file and made available to the public. Without this properly documented and verifiable annual certification, the Service would be unable to issue the requested import permit. This annual certification is specifically for requests to import live, wild-sourced African elephants or African elephant sport-hunted trophies.
Information to be collected from the range country for the import of live, wild-sourced elephants includes specific information on whether family units were kept intact and whether any of the animals collected are pregnant. Alternatively, information collected for the import of sport-hunted trophies includes specific information on the use of the meat of the animal.
Proposed Revisions
With this submission, based on feedback from our targeted outreach to nine individuals (the maximum allowed limit) familiar with this collection, we propose the following revisions to Form 3-200-37h to clarify requested information, improve clarity and sustainability, and to reduce burden:
(1) Remove the duplicative request for the mailing address from Part I, question 1, while retaining the expedited shipping instructions;
(2) Clarify question 2 so that the applicant identifies the application-specific contact, if it differs from the institution's primary contact;
(3) Remove duplicative funding language from question 29 and retain Question 30 as the separate funding question;
(4) Revise question 19 to clarify the information requested concerning anticipated effects of a proposed transfer on elephants currently housed at the facility and any resulting planned transfers; and
(5) Correct the identified typographical errors and the link to the list of designated ports.

AGENCY:
Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
This notice updates the October 20, 2026 notice announcing the appointment of members of the Fiscal Year (FY) 2026 Senior Executive Service (SES) Performance Review Boards (PRBs) for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).
DATES:
This notice is applicable as of November 4, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Christian Fajardo, Human Resources Specialist, Office of the Chief Human Capital Officer,
christian.fajardo@hq.dhs.gov
,
771-200-0392.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice updates the notice published on October 20, 2026 at
91 FR 66345
, to correct one name to the FY 2026 SES PRBs for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The purpose of the PRBs is to make recommendations to the appointing authority (
i.e.,
Agency Head) on the performance of senior executives (career and limited term appointees), including recommendations on performance ratings, performance-based pay adjustments, and performance awards. The PRBs will also make recommendations on the performance of Transportation Security Executive Service, Senior-Level, and Scientific and Professional employees. To make its recommendations, the PRBs will review performance appraisals, initial summary ratings, any response by the employee, and any higher-level official's recommendation.
In accordance with
5 U.S.C. 4314(c)
and
5 CFR 430.311
, each agency must establish one or more PRBs to make recommendations to the appointing authority (
i.e.,
Agency Head) on the performance of its senior executives. Each PRB must consist of three or more members. More than one-half of the membership of a PRB must be SES career appointees when reviewing appraisals and recommending performance-based pay adjustments or performance awards for career appointees. Composition of the PRB will be determined from among the individuals listed below:

AGENCY:
Drug Enforcement Administration, Department of Justice.
ACTION:
Final rule; technical amendment.
SUMMARY:
This final rule updates a Drug Enforcement Administration regulation to clarify that the provision regarding amendments to and withdrawal of registration applications also applies to applications for registration renewal. This action makes no substantive changes to this regulation.
DATES:
This rule is effective November 4, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Heather E. Achbach, Regulatory Drafting and Policy Support Section, Diversion Control Division, Drug Enforcement Administration; Mailing Address: 8701 Morrissette Drive, Springfield, Virginia 22152; Telephone: (571) 776-3882.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Legal Authority
The Controlled Substances Act (CSA) grants the Attorney General authority to promulgate and enforce rules and regulations pertaining to the registration and control of the manufacture, distribution, and dispensing of controlled substances and the maintenance and submission of records and reports related thereto.
[
1
]
The CSA further authorizes the Attorney General to promulgate regulations necessary and appropriate to execute the functions of subchapter I (Control and Enforcement) and subchapter II (Import and Export) of the CSA.
[
2
]
The Attorney General has delegated this authority to the Administrator of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA).
[
3
]
Technical Amendment
DEA regulations state that an application shall be deemed to be withdrawn if an applicant requests an application to be returned, or if an applicant fails to respond to official correspondence regarding the application when sent by registered or certified mail, return receipt requested.
[
4
]
The use of the term “applicant” may inadvertently suggest that this provision applies only to new registration applications and is not applicable to registration renewal applications. In this final rule, DEA is adding “or registrant” after “applicant” in
21 CFR 1301.16(b)
to clarify that this provision regarding amendments to and withdrawal of registration applications applies to both registration and registration renewal applications.
Regulatory Analyses
Administrative Procedure Act
An agency may find good cause to exempt a rule from certain provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), including those requiring the publication of a prior notice of proposed rulemaking and the opportunity for public comment, if such actions are determined to be unnecessary, impracticable, or contrary to the public interest.
[
5
]
The “unnecessary” prong of the APA good cause provision covers amendments that are “ `minor or merely technical' and of little public interest,”
[
6
]
or that involve “routine determination[s], insignificant in nature and impact, and inconsequential to the industry . . . and to the public.”
[
7
]
This rule contains only a technical amendment: it merely resolves a potential ambiguity by clarifying that the DEA regulation
[
8
]
regarding amendments to and withdrawal of applications applies to both registration and registration renewal applications. DEA has always understood and applied the regulation at
21 CFR 1301.16(b)
to include renewals. DEA has accordingly determined that notice and comment are not required.
Similarly, the APA provides that a delayed effective date is unnecessary when the agency finds good cause for dispensing with the delay. The APA's delayed-effective-date provision is intended “to give affected parties time to adjust their behavior before the final rule takes effect.”
[
9
]
Here, regulated parties will not need any time to adjust their behavior to the changes made in this final rule because the rule does no more than ensure that the regulatory text of
21 CFR 1301.16(b)
more clearly indicates the way that DEA has always understood and applied that provision.
In addition, the APA excepts from the requirements of notice and comment and a delayed effective date those rules that are non-substantive.
[
10
]
Substantive rules make “substantive changes in prior regulations” or “create new law, rights, or duties.”
[
11
]
Here, as already explained, this final rule makes no substantive changes in DEA's regulations because this rule simply clarifies the way that
21 CFR 1301.16(b)
has always been understood and applied.
Executive Orders 12866, 13563, and 14192 (Regulatory Review)
DEA has determined that this rulemaking is not a “significant regulatory action” under section 3(f) of Executive Order (E.O.) 12866 (Regulatory Planning and Review). Accordingly, this final rule has not been submitted to the Office of Management and Budget for review. This final rule was developed in accordance with section 1(b) of
E.O. 12866
, section 1(b) of
E.O. 13563
(Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review), and
E.O. 14192
(Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation).
As stated above, this final rule is a technical amendment to clarify that the provision regarding amendments to and withdrawal of registration applications also applies to applications for registration renewal. DEA has always applied this provision to both new and renewal applications, and therefore, this final rule does not impose any new or substantive requirements on the public or DEA registrants. DEA anticipates that
(
printed page 69501)
this final rule will have no economic impact.
This rule is not subject to
E.O. 14192
because it is neither a significant regulatory action under section 3(f) of
E.O. 12866
nor a significant guidance document that has been reviewed by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs.
[
12
]
Executive Order 12988
, Civil Justice Reform
This final rule meets the applicable standards set forth in sections 3(a) and 3(b)(2) of
E.O. 12988
to eliminate ambiguity, minimize litigation, establish clear legal standards, and reduce burdens.
Executive Order 13132
, Federalism
This final rule does not have federalism implications warranting the application of
E.O. 13132
. The final rule does not have substantial direct effects on the States, on the relationship between the Federal Government and the States, or the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.
Executive Order 13175
, Consultation and Coordination With Indian Tribal Governments
This final rule does not have tribal implications warranting the application of
E.O. 13175
. It does not have substantial direct effects on one or more Indian Tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and the Tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal government and Indian Tribes.
Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) (
5 U.S.C. 601-612
) applies to rules that are subject to notice and comment under section 553(b) of the APA. As explained above, DEA was not required to publish a general notice of proposed rulemaking prior to this final rule. Consequently, the RFA does not apply to this final rule.
Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995
In accordance with the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (UMRA),
2 U.S.C. 1501
et seq.,
DEA has determined that this action will not result in any Federal mandate that may result in the expenditure by State, local, and Tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, of $100 million or more (adjusted for inflation) in any one year. Therefore, neither a Small Government Agency Plan nor any other action is required under UMRA.
Executive Order 14267
, Reducing Anti-Competitive Regulatory Barriers
This final rule does not reduce competition, entrepreneurship, and innovation.
Executive Order 14294
, Fighting Overcriminalization of Federal Regulations
E.O. 14294
specifies that all notices of proposed rulemaking and final rules published in the FR, the violation of which may constitute a criminal regulatory offense, should include a statement identifying that the rule or proposed rule is a criminal regulatory offense, the authorizing statute, and the mens rea requirement for each element of the offense. This final rule does not involve a criminal regulatory offense and thus
E.O. 14294
does not apply.
Paperwork Reduction Act
This final rule does not impose a new collection of information requirement or modify an existing collection of information requirement under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995,
44 U.S.C. 3501-3521
. This final rule does not impose recordkeeping or reporting requirements on State or local governments, individuals, businesses, or organizations.
Congressional Review Act
This is not a major rule as defined by the Congressional Review Act (CRA),
5 U.S.C. 804
. This final rule will not result in an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more; a major increase in costs or prices; or significant adverse effects on competition, employment, investment, productivity, innovation, or the ability of United States-based companies to compete with foreign-based companies in domestic and export markets. However, pursuant to the CRA, DEA is submitting a copy of this final rule to both Houses of Congress and to the Comptroller General.

21 CFR Part 1301

Drug traffic control
Exports
Imports
