Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106783; File No. SR-NASDAQ-2026-093]
October 30, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1)
[
1
]
of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”)
[
2
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
3
]
notice is hereby given that on October 22, 2026, The Nasdaq Stock Market LLC (“Nasdaq” or “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II, and III below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to amend the Exchange's transaction fees at Equity 7, Sections 115 and 130, to delete obsolete references to the CORE FIX order entry protocol.
The text of the proposed rule change is available on the Exchange's website at
https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/​rulebook/​nasdaq/​rulefilings
,
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
(
printed page 69584)
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and the Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The purpose of the proposed rule change is to amend the Exchange's transaction fees at Nasdaq Equity 7, Sections 115 and 130, to remove obsolete references to the CORE FIX order entry protocol.
On October 22, 2026, the Exchange filed with the Commission a proposal, with immediate effectiveness, to abandon plans to deploy the CORE FIX order entry protocol. The Exchange now proposes to delete from its equities fee schedule (Nasdaq Equity 7) all references to CORE FIX, which had been added to the fee schedule in anticipation of testing and deploying CORE FIX.
Specifically, the Exchange proposes to make the following changes:
1. In Equity 7, Section 115(f)(1), remove the reference and associated price for CORE FIX, including the tags to notes “1” and “**”, as well as the corresponding notes “1” and “**”. This rule established a fee of $575, per month, per port, for CORE FIX.
a. Note “1” read “
Temporary 30-Day Fee Waiver for CORE FIX Ports. The Exchange shall offer users a 30-day waiver of the CORE FIX port fee for up to five newly added CORE FIX ports. This fee waiver shall be offered for a three-month period, beginning on the date when CORE FIX first becomes available on the Exchange, which such date the Exchange shall announce in an Equity Trader Alert.
”
b. And Note “**” read “
Subject to Exchange Rule Equity 1, Section 1(a)(19), the first five Night Session CORE FIX ports ordered for an MPID will be provided without charge. Beginning with the sixth Night Session CORE FIX port ordered for the same MPID, the Exchange will assess the standard fee otherwise applicable to CORE FIX ports under this Section 115(g) of Rule Equity 7.
”
2. In Equity 7, Section 130(d)(1)(B), remove the tag to note “1”, as well as the corresponding note “1”. This rule establishes, in relevant part, a fee of $300 per port, per month, for subscribers that conduct tests of their access protocol connections through the Nasdaq Testing Facility. Note “1” read “
Temporary 30-Day Fee Waiver for CORE FIX NTF Ports. The Exchange shall offer subscribers a 30-day waiver of the $300 NTF fee in this paragraph (d)(1)(B) of Section 130 for up to five newly added CORE FIX NTF ports. This fee waiver shall be offered for a three-month period, beginning on a date to be specified by the Exchange in an Equity Trader Alert.
”
3. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that its proposal is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act,
[
4
]
in general, and furthers the objectives of Sections 6(b)(4) and 6(b)(5) of the Act,
[
5
]
in particular, in that it provides for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees and other charges among members and issuers and other persons using any facility, and is not designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers.
The Exchange's proposed changes to its schedule of credits are reasonable in several respects. As a threshold matter, the Exchange is subject to significant competitive forces in the market for equity securities transaction services that constrain its pricing determinations in that market. The fact that this market is competitive has long been recognized by the courts. In
NetCoalition
v.
Securities and Exchange Commission,
the D.C. Circuit stated as follows: “[n]o one disputes that competition for order flow is `fierce.' . . . As the SEC explained, `[i]n the U.S. national market system, buyers and sellers of securities, and the broker-dealers that act as their order-routing agents, have a wide range of choices of where to route orders for execution'; [and] `no exchange can afford to take its market share percentages for granted' because `no exchange possesses a monopoly, regulatory or otherwise, in the execution of order flow from broker dealers'. . . .”
[
6
]
The Commission and the courts have repeatedly expressed their preference for competition over regulatory intervention in determining prices, products, and services in the securities markets. In Regulation NMS, while adopting a series of steps to improve the current market model, the Commission highlighted the importance of market forces in determining prices and SRO revenues and, also, recognized that current regulation of the market system “has been remarkably successful in promoting market competition in its broader forms that are most important to investors and listed companies.”
[
7
]
Numerous indicia demonstrate the competitive nature of this market. For example, clear substitutes to the Exchange exist in the market for equity security transaction services. The Exchange is only one of several equity venues to which market participants may direct their order flow. Competing equity exchanges offer similar tiered pricing structures to that of the Exchange, including schedules of incentives and fees that apply based upon members achieving certain volume thresholds.
Within this environment, market participants can freely and often do shift their order flow among the Exchange and competing venues in response to changes in their respective pricing schedules. As such, the proposal represents a reasonable attempt by the Exchange to increase its liquidity and market share relative to its competitors.
The Exchange's proposal is also reasonable, equitable and not unfairly discriminatory because it removes obsolete references to CORE FIX and related temporary waiver language from the fee schedule. The Exchange has determined not to deploy CORE FIX, and the provisions proposed for deletion therefore would not govern an active protocol or an active fee offering. Removing references to the CORE FIX port fee, Night Session CORE FIX ports, and CORE FIX NTF ports will not change the availability, pricing, or functionality of any service currently used by members, and will apply equally to all market participants. Instead, the proposal will make Equity 7, Sections 115 and 130 easier to navigate, understand, and administer by eliminating text that could otherwise create confusion regarding unavailable protocol functionality, obsolete fees, and waiver language that will not apply. For these reasons, the Exchange believes that the proposal is consistent with an equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees, and other charges and is not designed to permit unfair discrimination.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. In terms of inter-market competition, the Exchange notes that it operates in a highly competitive market in which market participants can readily favor competing venues if they deem fee levels at a particular venue to be excessive, or incentive opportunities available at other venues to be more favorable. In such an environment, the Exchange must continually adjust its fees to
(
printed page 69585)
remain competitive with other exchanges and with alternative trading systems that have been exempted from compliance with the statutory standards applicable to exchanges. Because competitors are free to modify their own fees in response, and because market participants may readily adjust their order routing practices, the Exchange believes that the degree to which fee changes in this market may impose any burden on competition is extremely limited.
The proposal will not impose an undue burden on inter-market or intra-market competition. The proposed deletions are not designed to address a competitive issue, but rather to ensure that the Exchange's fee schedule accurately reflects the protocols and fees currently available to market participants. Because CORE FIX will not be deployed, no market participant will lose access to an available protocol, lose an applicable waiver, or become subject to a new or changed fee as a result of deleting the obsolete CORE FIX production, Night Session, and NTF references. The deletions will apply uniformly to all members and other market participants and will not disadvantage any category of Exchange participant. To the contrary, removing obsolete and inapplicable text will promote a clearer and more transparent fee schedule for all participants.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
No written comments were either solicited or received.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The foregoing rule change has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(ii) of the Act.
[
8
]
At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is: (i) necessary or appropriate in the public interest; (ii) for the protection of investors; or (iii) otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-NASDAQ-2026-093 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-NASDAQ-2026-093. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-NASDAQ-2026-093 and should be submitted on or before November 25, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
9
]
Sherry R. Haywood,
Assistant Secretary.

In Equity 7, Section 3, under Port Fees, remove the reference and associated price for CORE FIX, including the tag to note “1” (which was incorrectly attached to the price for OUCH, another order entry protocol offered by the Exchange), as well as the corresponding note “1”. This rule established, in relevant part, a fee for CORE FIX of $400, per month, per port. Note “1” read
“Temporary 30-Day Fee Waiver for CORE FIX Ports. The Exchange shall offer users a 30-day waiver of the CORE FIX port fee for up to five newly added CORE FIX ports. This fee waiver shall be offered for a three-month period, beginning on October 10, 2022.”
2. In Equity 7, Section 3, under Port Fees, remove the reference to CORE FIX in the line-item concerning “Disaster recovery port.” This rule established, in relevant part, a fee of $25, per month, per port, for a CORE FIX disaster recovery port.
3. In Equity 7, Section 3, under Testing Facilities, remove the tag to note “1”, as well as the corresponding note “1”. This rule establishes, in relevant part, a fee of $300 per port, per month, for subscribers that conduct tests of their access protocol connections through the Exchange Testing Facility. Note “1” read
“Temporary 30-Day Fee Waiver for CORE FIX Testing Facility Ports. The Exchange shall offer subscribers a 30-day waiver of the $300 Testing Facility fee in this paragraph (a) for up to five newly added CORE FIX Testing Facility ports. This fee waiver shall be offered for a three-month period, beginning on September 22, 2022.”
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that its proposal is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act,
[
4
]
in general, and furthers the objectives of Sections 6(b)(4) and 6(b)(5) of the Act,
[
5
]
in particular, in that it provides for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees and other charges among members and issuers and other persons using any facility, and is not designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers.
The Exchange's proposed changes to its schedule of credits are reasonable in several respects. As a threshold matter, the Exchange is subject to significant competitive forces in the market for equity securities transaction services that constrain its pricing determinations in that market. The fact that this market is competitive has long been recognized by the courts. In
NetCoalition
v.
Securities and Exchange Commission,
the D.C. Circuit stated as follows: “[n]o one disputes that competition for order flow is `fierce.' . . . As the SEC explained, `[i]n the U.S. national market system, buyers and sellers of securities, and the broker-dealers that act as their order-routing agents, have a wide range of choices of where to route orders for execution'; [and] `no exchange can afford to take its market share percentages for granted' because `no exchange possesses a monopoly, regulatory or otherwise, in the execution of order flow from broker dealers'. . . .”
[
6
]
The Commission and the courts have repeatedly expressed their preference for competition over regulatory intervention in determining prices, products, and services in the securities markets. In Regulation NMS, while adopting a series of steps to improve the current market model, the Commission highlighted the importance of market forces in determining prices and SRO revenues and, also, recognized that current regulation of the market system “has been remarkably successful in promoting market competition in its broader forms that are most important to investors and listed companies.”
[
7
]
Numerous indicia demonstrate the competitive nature of this market. For example, clear substitutes to the Exchange exist in the market for equity security transaction services. The Exchange is only one of several equity venues to which market participants may direct their order flow. Competing equity exchanges offer similar tiered pricing structures to that of the Exchange, including schedules of rebates and fees that apply based upon members achieving certain volume thresholds.
Within this environment, market participants can freely and often do shift their order flow among the Exchange and competing venues in response to changes in their respective pricing schedules. As such, the proposal represents a reasonable attempt by the Exchange to increase its liquidity and market share relative to its competitors.
The Exchange's proposal is also reasonable, equitable and not unfairly discriminatory because it removes obsolete references to CORE FIX and related temporary waiver language from the fee schedule. The Exchange has determined not to deploy CORE FIX, and the provisions proposed for deletion therefore would not govern an active protocol or an active fee offering. Removing references to the CORE FIX production port fee, CORE FIX disaster recovery port fee, CORE FIX Testing Facility ports, and related temporary waiver language will not change the availability, pricing, or functionality of any service currently used by members, and will apply equally to all market participants. Instead, the proposal will make Equity 7, Section 3 easier to navigate, understand, and administer by eliminating text that could otherwise create confusion regarding unavailable protocol functionality, obsolete fees, and waiver language that will not apply. For these reasons, the Exchange believes that the proposal is consistent with an equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees, and other charges and is not designed to permit unfair discrimination.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. In terms of inter-market competition, the Exchange notes that it operates in a highly competitive market in which market participants can readily favor competing venues if they deem fee levels at a particular venue to be excessive, or rebate opportunities available at other venues to be more favorable. In such an environment, the Exchange must continually adjust its fees to remain competitive with other exchanges and with alternative trading systems that
(
printed page 69589)
have been exempted from compliance with the statutory standards applicable to exchanges. Because competitors are free to modify their own fees in response, and because market participants may readily adjust their order routing practices, the Exchange believes that the degree to which fee changes in this market may impose any burden on competition is extremely limited.
The proposal will not impose an undue burden on inter-market or intra-market competition. The proposed deletions are not designed to address a competitive issue, but rather to ensure that the Exchange's fee schedule accurately reflects the protocols and fees currently available to market participants. Because CORE FIX will not be deployed, no market participant will lose access to an available protocol, lose an applicable waiver, or become subject to a new or changed fee as a result of deleting the obsolete CORE FIX production, disaster recovery, Testing Facility, and waiver references. The deletions will apply uniformly to all members and other market participants and will not disadvantage any category of Exchange participant. To the contrary, removing obsolete and inapplicable text will promote a clearer and more transparent fee schedule for all participants.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
No written comments were either solicited or received.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The foregoing rule change has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(ii) of the Act.
[
8
]
At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is: (i) necessary or appropriate in the public interest; (ii) for the protection of investors; or (iii) otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-PHLX-2026-66  on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-PHLX-2026-66. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-PHLX-2026-66 and should be submitted on or before November 25, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
9
]
Sherry R. Haywood,
Assistant Secretary.

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106780; File No. SR-ISE-2026-53]
October 30, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”),
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on October 19, 2026, Nasdaq ISE, LLC (“ISE” or “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I and II below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to amend the strike intervals for options on certain Exchange-Traded Fund Shares (“ETFs”).
(
printed page 69597)
The text of the proposed rule change is available on the Exchange's website at
https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/​rulebook/​ise/​rulefilings
,
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to amend Options 4, Section 5, Series of Options Contracts Open for Trading, to revise certain strike intervals applicable to options on ETFs that are more than one month and less than nine months from expiration and to make related organizational changes to that section. The Exchange also proposes to amend the rule text related to Qualifying Securities in Supplementary Material .03 to Options 4, Section 5 (Short Term Options Series Program).
Background
Currently, Options 4, Section 5(d) provides that, except as otherwise provided in the Supplementary Material thereto, the interval between strike prices of series of options on individual stocks will be:
(1) $2.50 or greater where the strike price is $25.00 or less;
(2) $5.00 or greater where the strike price is greater than $25.00; and
(3) $10.00 or greater where the strike price is greater than $200.00.
Current Section 5(e) separately provides that options on SPDR S&P 500 ETF (“SPY”), iShares Core S&P 500 ETF (“IVV”), PowerShares QQQ Trust (“QQQ”), iShares Russell 2000 Index Fund (“IWM”), SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (“DIA”), and SPDR® Gold Trust (“GLD”) (collectively “enumerated ETFs”), may be listed at $1 or greater intervals; Section 5(e) applies only to the aforementioned ETFs. The unlettered paragraph of Section 5(d) generally provides $1 or greater intervals for ETFs where the strike price is $200 or less and $5.00 or greater intervals where the strike price is greater than $200.
Additionally, currently Supplementary Material .03(e) to Options 4, Section 5 permits the Exchange to open for trading Short Term Option Series at strike price intervals of (i) $0.50 or greater where the strike price is less than $100, and $1 or greater where the strike price is between $100 and $150 for all option classes that participate in the Short Term Options Series Program; (ii) $0.50 for option classes that trade in one dollar increments and are in the Short Term Option Series Program; or (iii) $2.50 or greater where the strike price is above $150.
Today, the Exchange's listing rules at Supplementary Material .03 to Options 4, Section 5 permit the listing of additional expirations on eligible individual stocks or Exchange-Traded Fund Shares that meet certain criteria on a quarterly basis (“Qualifying Securities”). Specifically, as measured on the last day of the prior calendar quarter, an underlying security must have either (A) a market capitalization greater than 700 billion dollars for an individual stock, based on the closing price, or (B) Assets under Management (“AUM”) greater than 50 billion dollars (under (B)(i)) or greater than 25 billion dollars (under (B)(ii)) for an Exchange-Traded Fund Share, based on net asset value (“NAV”). Further, eligible individual stocks or ETFs must have monthly options volume, as measured by sides traded in the last month preceding the quarter end, of greater than 10 million options, or greater than 5 million options for an Exchange-Traded Fund Share that qualified under (B)(ii) of the Qualifying Securities criteria; must have a position limit of at least 250,000 contracts; and must participate in the Penny Interval Program.
[
3
]
Each calendar quarter, the Exchange applies the Qualifying Securities criteria to individual stocks and ETFs to determine eligibility for the following quarter as a Qualifying Security. Beginning on the second trading day in the first month of each calendar quarter, the market capitalization of individual stocks is calculated based on the closing price established on the primary exchange on the last trading day of the prior calendar quarter and the AUM for ETFs is calculated based on the NAV established on the primary exchange on the last trading day of the prior calendar quarter.
[
4
]
Proposal
At this time, the Exchange proposes to amend Options 4, Section 5, Series of Options Contracts Open for Trading. Specifically, the Exchange proposes to incorporate current Options 4, Section 5(e) into Options 4, Section 5(d) and remove the “(e)” designation so that it becomes unlettered text within Section 5(d). Under the proposal, the general $1-or-greater interval for ETFs where the strike price is $200 or less and the $5.00-or-greater interval where the strike price is greater than $200, as well as the $1-or-greater interval for the enumerated ETFs, will remain unchanged, except that ETF Qualifying Securities may be listed at $0.50 or greater intervals where the strike price is less than $100, as described below.
[
5
]
The Exchange also proposes to amend current Options 4, Section 5(e) to remove the clause “Notwithstanding any other provision regarding the interval of strike prices of series of options on Exchange-Traded Fund Shares in this Rule,” and to amend certain ETF names to reflect the current name.
[
6
]
So that the first sentence of the proposed unlettered paragraph states, “The interval of strike prices on SPDR S&P 500 ETF (“SPY”), iShares Core S&P 500 ETF (“IVV”), PowerShares QQQ Trust (“QQQ”), iShares Russell 2000 Index Fund (“IWM”), the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (“DIA”), and SPDR® Gold Trust (“GLD”) options will be $1 or greater.” The Exchange
(
printed page 69598)
proposes to add new sentences to the end of that proposed unlettered paragraph that state,
Further, notwithstanding any other provision in this Rule regarding the interval of strike prices of series of options on Exchange-Traded Fund Shares, the interval of strike prices for options on an Exchange-Traded Fund Share that is a Qualifying Security under Supplementary Material .03 to Options 4, Section 5 will be $0.50 or greater where the strike price is less than $100, but only for a calendar quarter for which the Exchange has determined that the Exchange-Traded Fund Share satisfies each of the Qualifying Securities criteria. If an Exchange-Traded Fund Share ceases to meet the criteria of a Qualifying Security, any series of options listed at $0.50 strike price intervals under this paragraph may remain listed, but the Exchange may not list additional series of options until the Exchange-Traded Fund Share again meets the criteria of a Qualifying Security.
The Exchange's proposal is designed to fill the gap between existing listing rules such that options on ETF Qualifying Securities
[
7
]
may list $0.50 strike intervals where the strike price is less than $100 for options that are more than one month and less than nine months
[
8
]
from expiration.
Further, the Exchange proposes conforming organizational changes to Options 4, Section 5. The existing intervals for individual stocks in Section 5(d) are designated as subparagraphs (1) through (3). The current subsection (e) designation is removed; former subsection (f) is renumbered as subparagraph (d)(i), titled “Volatility Indexes:” with conforming cross-reference amendments; former subsection (h) is renumbered as subparagraph (d)(ii) and titled “Index-Linked Securities”; and former subsection (i) is renumbered as subparagraph (d)(iii). Former subsection (j) is renumbered as (e); former subsection (k) is renumbered as (f); and former subsection (g) is relocated to the end of Section 5 as new subsection (g).
ETF Qualifying Securities are highly liquid and actively traded, and only a select group of ETFs meets the stringent requirements. ETF Qualifying Securities occupy a unique position at the top of the ETF liquidity spectrum and are readily distinguishable from the broader population of ETFs. The 250,000-contract position limit is the highest position limit under Exchange rules; options that qualify for this limit are highly liquid securities that have met stringent requirements. Additionally, in order to qualify for the Penny Interval Program, an options class must be among the 300 most actively traded multiply listed option classes overlying securities priced below $200. Permitting $0.50 strike intervals for ETF Qualifying Securities for expirations more than one month and less than nine months away under Options 4, Section 5(d) is reasonable because these instruments possess sufficient liquidity to support finer strike granularity without adverse effects on market quality.
The proposed change reflects that ETFs increasingly trade at lower dollar prices than traditional large-cap equities and market-cap-weighted index ETFs, particularly narrower thematic, sector, commodity, currency, and single-country products. ETF Qualifying Securities span a broad range of asset classes, including domestic and international equity, fixed income, commodities, currencies, and alternative strategies, and are widely used by retail and institutional investors alike to obtain diversified, low-cost exposure. For ETF Qualifying Securities trading below $100, the current $1 minimum interval for expirations more than one month away, beyond what can be listed today for ETFs in the Short Term Options Series Program, represents a percentage move in the underlying that materially exceeds the corresponding percentage move for higher-priced securities. For example, a $1 interval on a $50 ETF represents a 2% move in the underlying, whereas a $1 interval on a $200 ETF represents only a 0.5% move. By contrast, a $0.50 interval on a $50 ETF represents a 1% move, and a $0.50 interval on a $25 ETF represents a 2% move. The proposed $0.50 interval would produce percentage moves that are more consistent across the price spectrum and more closely aligned with the daily and long-term price behavior of many ETFs.
The Exchange believes that the absence of $0.50 strike price intervals below $100 in ETF Qualifying Securities for expirations more than one month and less than nine months away significantly constrains investors' hedging and trading opportunities. Investors commonly use expirations in this aforementioned timeframe to hedge or express a view on a position over a multi-month horizon, such as protecting a holding through a quarter-end or an anticipated market event. Because these positions are held longer and are often sized to a specific risk tolerance, the precision of the strike price is economically meaningful: a strike that is too far from the investor's target level either leaves unwanted exposure unhedged or requires the investor to pay for more protection than needed. Today, $0.50 intervals below $100 are available for ETFs only in the Short Term Option Series Program, for options with one month or less to expiration, so investors seeking comparable precision over a longer horizon have no listed alternative. The Exchange proposes to extend the $0.50 interval only to the select group of ETFs that qualify as ETF Qualifying Securities. These ETFs sit at the top of the ETF liquidity spectrum: each must have AUM greater than $25 billion, meet substantial monthly options volume thresholds, carry the highest position limit permitted under Exchange rules (250,000 contracts), and participate in the Penny Interval Program. This liquidity supports finer strike granularity without adverse effects on market quality. The proposal is also consistent with the treatment of SPY, one of the most liquid ETFs, which may be listed at $1 or greater intervals at all strike prices. Because SPY trades at a high dollar price, a $1 interval represents only a small fraction of a percent of the underlying's value. ETF Qualifying Securities trading below $100 warrant comparable precision: the proposed $0.50 interval would result in at-the-money series based on the underlying ETF moving 1% or less for underlyings priced at or above $50, and reasonably small percentage moves for underlyings priced below $50. For example, an investor holding an ETF Qualifying Security trading at $50 who seeks to protect against a decline of more than 5% through an expiration four months away would want a $47.50 put. Under the current $1 interval, the investor must choose between a $47 put, which leaves an additional 1% of downside unprotected, and a $48 put, which costs more than the protection requires. The proposed $0.50 interval would allow the investor to purchase the $47.50 put and hedge precisely to the desired level. The Exchange believes that the proposed strike-setting regime is consistent with the more measured price movements typical of broad-based and diversified ETFs.
Considering the fact that many ETF Qualifying Securities consistently trade at price levels below $100, and that the current $1 minimum interval may result in at-the-money and near-the-money series being spaced more widely than investors require to manage risk, the Exchange believes that continuing to maintain the current $1 minimum interval below $100 may have a negative
(
printed page 69599)
effect on investing, trading, and hedging opportunities, and volume. The Exchange believes that the investing, trading, and hedging opportunities available with options on ETF Qualifying Securities far outweigh any potential negative impact of allowing such options to trade in more finely tailored intervals below the $100 price point.
The proposed strike-setting regime would permit strikes to be set to reflect the value of the underlying more closely and allow investors and traders to roll open positions from a lower strike to a higher strike in conjunction with the price movements of the underlying ETF. Under the current rule, where the next higher available series would be $1 away from, for example, a $50 strike, an investor would need for the underlying product to move 2%—from $50 to $51—before executing a roll up. With the proposed rule change, the investor would be able to roll an open options position from a $50 strike to a $50.50 strike, which is only a 1% move for the underlying. As a result, the proposed rule change will allow the Exchange to better respond to customer demand for ETF strike prices more precisely aligned with the smaller, incremental price movements typical of ETF Qualifying Securities.
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change, like the other strike price programs currently offered by the Exchange, will benefit investors by providing investors the flexibility to tailor their investment and hedging decisions using options more closely on ETF Qualifying Securities. Moreover, by allowing series of such options to be listed at $0.50 intervals below $100, the proposal will moderately augment the potential total number of options series available on the Exchange. However, the Exchange believes it and the Options Price Reporting Authority (“OPRA”) have the necessary systems capacity to handle any potential additional traffic associated with this proposed rule change. The Exchange also believes that Members will not have a capacity issue due to the proposed rule change. In addition, the Exchange represents that it does not believe that this expansion will cause fragmentation of liquidity, but rather, believes that finer strike intervals will serve to increase liquidity available as well as price efficiency by providing more trading opportunities for all market participants.
To mitigate the potential for excessive series proliferation, the Exchange will apply its existing series maintenance policies to options listed pursuant to the proposed $0.50 interval, including its policies governing the delisting of series with low or no open interest. The Exchange will monitor the impact of the proposed rule change on trading volume, quotation traffic, and open interest, and will report to the Commission upon request.
Qualifying Securities Amendment
The Exchange also proposes to amend the rule text related to “Qualifying Securities” in Supplementary Material .03 to Options 4, Section 5, which governs the Exchange's Short Term Option Series Program.
[
9
]
The amendment seeks to clarify the applicability of Table 1 Short Term Option Daily Expirations as compared to Table 2. Under Supplementary Material .03 of Options 4, Section 5, the Exchange may list Short Term Option Weekly Expirations that expire on each of the next five Fridays that are business days, excluding Fridays on which standard, Monthly Options Series, or Quarterly Options Series expirations occur. The Exchange may also list series of options on the symbols in Table 1 and pursuant to the criteria noted in Table 2 of Supplementary Material .03 that expire at the close of business on each of the next two Mondays, Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Thursdays that are business days beyond the current week (“Short Term Option Daily Expirations”). The Exchange may have no more than two Short Term Option Daily Expirations beyond the current week for each of those days at one time.
Currently, Table 1 lists specific symbols and the number of Short Term Option Daily Expirations each may trade on each day.
[
10
]
Table 2 does not list specific symbols, rather it sets out the expirations available to categories of “Qualifying Securities” which are required to meet certain criteria on a quarterly basis to qualify for certain expirations.
[
11
]
Currently, the rule text states that,
Qualifying Securities are defined as eligible individual stocks or Exchange-Traded Fund Shares, which are separate and apart from the symbols listed in Table 1, that have received approval to list additional expiries on specific symbols, that meet the following criteria on a quarterly basis:
The Exchange proposes to amend the rule text to instead provide,
Qualifying Securities are individual stocks and Exchange-Traded Fund Shares that satisfy each of the following criteria on a quarterly basis. Options on the symbols listed in Table 1 may trade the number of Short Term Option Daily Expirations, on the days set forth in Table 1, regardless of whether they satisfy the following criteria. A Qualifying Security may trade the number of Short Term Option Daily Expirations on the days set forth in Table 2 only for the calendar quarter for which the Exchange has determined that it satisfies each of the following criteria. If a symbol listed in Table 1 is also a Qualifying Security, the Exchange may list, for each day, the greater of the number of Short Term Option Daily Expirations set forth in Table 1 and the number set forth in Table 2. The criteria are as follows:
The expiration dates in Table 1 are not dependent on the Table 1 symbols meeting the criteria for a Qualifying Security. By way of example, shares of the SPDR® Gold Trust (“GLD”) are Exchange-Traded Fund Shares under Options 4, Section 3(h)(iv). GLD is also listed by name in Table 1, which permits two Monday and two Wednesday Short Term Option Daily Expirations. Every quarter the Exchange may list two Monday and two Wednesday expirations for GLD under Table 1. In a quarter in which GLD meets the (B)(i) criteria, the Exchange may also list two Tuesday and two Thursday expirations under Table 2. If, in the following quarter, GLD fails a Qualifying Securities criterion, the Exchange may not list the Tuesday and Thursday expirations, but may retain the Monday and Wednesday expirations. Therefore, GLD always has its Table 1 expirations and may also have Table 2 expirations in any calendar quarter in which it satisfies each of the Qualifying Securities criteria. The proposed rule text seeks to make the interaction between Table 1 and Table
(
printed page 69600)
2 clear and does not substantively change the application of the rules.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that its proposal is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act,
[
12
]
in general, and furthers the objectives of Section 6(b)(5) of the Act,
[
13
]
in particular, in that it is designed to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest. In particular, the proposed rule change will allow investors to use options on ETF Qualifying Securities more easily. The proposed rule change would allow investors to better trade and hedge positions in options on ETF Qualifying Securities where the strike price is less than $100 and that are more than one month and less than nine months from expiration, and would ensure that investors in such options are not at a disadvantage simply because the underlying trades below $100. Investors use these expirations to hedge or express a view over a multi-month horizon, where strike precision is economically meaningful, and today the $0.50 interval below $100 is available for ETFs only in the Short Term Option Series Program for expirations of one month or less. The proposal fills that gap and permits ETF Qualifying Securities to achieve percentage strike spacing comparable to that already available for the enumerated ETFs, such as SPY, at their higher prices. The proposed $0.50 strike interval on these uniquely liquid instruments will enhance hedging precision, promote price discovery, and remove an impediment to the efficient functioning of the options market.
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 6(b)(1) of the Act, which requires an exchange to be organized and have the capacity to carry out the purposes of the Act and the rules and regulations thereunder. The proposal would enable the Exchange to respond to customer demand for options on ETF Qualifying Securities to trade in $0.50 intervals below a $100 strike price. The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule would create additional capacity issues or affect market functionality. As noted above, options on ETF Qualifying Securities currently trade in $1 intervals at strike prices at or below $200 for expirations more than one month away. Because ETF Qualifying Securities frequently trade at prices below $100, that $1 minimum interval can produce percentage strike spacing that is materially wider than what investors and traders require to establish, roll, and manage risk. This proposal addresses that issue by establishing a $0.50 minimum interval below $100 for all ETF Qualifying Securities with more than one month and less than nine months to expiration on a class-neutral basis.
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change, like other strike-price programs currently offered by the Exchange, will benefit investors by giving them increased flexibility to tailor their investment and hedging decisions more closely. Applying the $0.50 interval to any ETF Qualifying Security, rather than specifically naming underlyings, avoids arbitrary distinctions between ETFs that are economically similar and allows the Exchange to keep pace with new ETFs approved for options trading without piecemeal rulemaking. Because ETF Qualifying Securities must already be approved for options trading pursuant to Options 4, Section 3(h) and satisfy the Qualifying Securities criteria, the underlyings eligible for the proposed $0.50 interval will have satisfied the same regulatory safeguards that apply to existing options on ETFs, including standards designed to ensure liquidity and transparency and to reduce susceptibility to manipulation of the underlying. Further, because eligibility is determined quarterly, any series listed at $0.50 intervals may remain listed if an ETF ceases to qualify, but no additional such series may be listed until the ETF again meets the Qualifying Securities criteria, which protects investors holding existing positions while limiting the $0.50 interval to ETFs that currently qualify.
ETF Qualifying Securities are highly liquid and actively traded, and only a select group of ETFs meets the stringent requirements, including a 250,000-contract position limit, the highest position limit under Exchange rules, and participation in the Penny Interval Program. Permitting $0.50 strike intervals for ETF Qualifying Securities for expirations more than one month and less than nine months away in Options 4, Section 5(d) is therefore reasonable because these instruments possess sufficient liquidity to support finer strike granularity without adverse effects on market quality.
With regard to the impact of this proposal on system capacity, the Exchange believes it and OPRA have the necessary systems capacity to handle any potential additional traffic associated with this proposed rule change. The Exchange believes that its Members will not have a capacity issue as a result of this proposal. In addition, the Exchange will apply its existing series maintenance policies, including its policies governing the delisting of series with low or no open interest, to mitigate the potential for excessive series proliferation.
Finally, the conforming organizational changes to Options 4, Section 5 are intended to bring greater clarity to the Exchange's rules by organizing the text in such a way as to group like concepts for greater readability. These proposed changes are consistent with the Act as they are non-substantive.
Qualifying Securities Amendment
The proposed amendment to Supplementary Material .03 to Options 4, Section 5 is consistent with the Act because the proposal makes clear and more transparent the rule text associated with Qualifying Securities. As amended, the rule text more directly provides that the Exchange may list Table 1 symbols for the days and expirations noted, regardless of the criteria applicable to Qualifying Securities. In contrast, the Exchange may list the days and expirations noted in Table 2 for a Qualifying Security, depending on which criteria are met, only for a quarter in which the security meets those criteria. The proposal is intended to reduce ambiguity, which removes impediments to and perfects the mechanism of a free and open market.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any intra-market burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The proposal does not remove or reduce any strike price interval currently available; it only permits additional, finer strike price intervals for options on ETF Qualifying Securities that are more than one month and less than nine months from expiration. The proposal will apply equally to all market participants and to every ETF that satisfies the Qualifying Securities criteria. Rather than burdening competition, the Exchange believes that the proposed rule change will result in additional investment options and opportunities to achieve the investment and trading objectives of market participants seeking efficient trading and hedging vehicles, to the benefit of investors, market participants, and the marketplace in general. In addition, the proposal will allow options on ETF
(
printed page 69601)
Qualifying Securities trading below $100 to achieve percentage strike spacing comparable to that already available for the enumerated ETFs, such as SPY, which are similarly popular and widely traded ETF products, permitting investors to employ similar investment and hedging strategies across these options.
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any inter-market burden on competition, as other options markets may adopt a similar rule.
Qualifying Securities Amendment
The proposal does not impose any intra-market burden on competition because the rule text is intended to clarify existing rules and does not substantively amend the rules. The proposal does not impose any inter-market burden on competition as other exchanges with the same rule are able to list identical options pursuant to Supplementary Material .03 to Options 4, Section 5.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
No written comments were either solicited or received.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
Within 45 days of the date of publication of this notice in the
Federal Register
or within such longer period up to 90 days (i) as the Commission may designate if it finds such longer period to be appropriate and publishes its reasons for so finding or (ii) as to which the self-regulatory organization consents, the Commission will:
(A) by order approve or disapprove such proposed rule change, or
(B) institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule change should be disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-ISE-2026-53 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-ISE-2026-53. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-ISE-2026-53 and should be submitted on or before November 25, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
14
]
Sherry R. Haywood,
Assistant Secretary.

title: Self-Regulatory Organizations: Long-Term Stock Exchange, Inc.; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of Proposed Rule Change To Amend LTSE Rule 3.291
full_text:

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106779; File No. SR-LTSE-2026-25]
October 30, 2026.
Pursuant to the provisions of Section 19(b)(1) under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”),
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on October 20, 2026, Long-Term Stock Exchange, Inc. (“LTSE” or the “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II and III below, which Items have been prepared by the self-regulatory organization. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange is filing with the Commission a proposed rule change to amend LTSE Rule 3.291, Influencing or Rewarding Employees of Others; Gratuities, to conform to the rules of the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, Inc. (“FINRA”) for purposes of an agreement between the Exchange and FINRA pursuant to Rule 17d-2 under the Act.
[
3
]
The text of the proposed rule change is available at the Exchange's website at
https://longtermstockexchange.com/​
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The self-regulatory organization has prepared summaries, set forth in Sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to amend LTSE Rule 3.291, Influencing or Rewarding Employees of Others; Gratuities, to conform the rule so that it is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220. The Exchange notes that this filing is based on a proposal recently submitted by FINRA, and approved by the Commission, to amend FINRA Rule 3220 (Influencing or Rewarding Employees of Others).
[
4
]
Pursuant to Rule 17d-2 under the Act,
[
5
]
the Exchange and FINRA entered into an agreement to allocate regulatory responsibility for common rules (the “17d-2 Agreement”). The 17d-2 Agreement covers common members of the Exchange and FINRA and allocates to FINRA regulatory responsibility, with respect to common members, for the following: (i) examination of common members of the Exchange and FINRA for compliance with certain federal securities laws, rules and regulations and rules of the Exchange that the Exchange has certified as identical or substantially similar to FINRA rules; (ii) investigation of common members of the Exchange and FINRA for violations of certain federal securities laws, rules or regulations, or Exchange rules that the Exchange has certified as identical or substantially similar to a FINRA rule; and (iii) enforcement of compliance by common members with certain federal securities laws, rules and regulations, and the rules of the Exchange that the Exchange has certified as identical or substantially similar to FINRA rules.
[
6
]
The 17d-2 Agreement included a certification by the Exchange that states that the requirements contained in certain Exchange rules are identical to, or substantially similar to, certain FINRA rules that have been identified as comparable. To conform to comparable FINRA rules for purposes of the 17d-2 Agreement, the Exchange proposes conforming the text of LTSE Rule 3.291 so that it is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220.
Currently, LTSE Rule 3.291 is excluded from the 17d-2 Agreement because it is not identical, or substantially similar, to FINRA Rule
(
printed page 69594)
3220. Current LTSE Rule 3.291 prohibits a Member or person associated with a Member from directly or indirectly, giving or permitting to be given anything of value, including gratuities, in excess of one hundred dollars per individual per year to any person, principal, proprietor, employee, agent or representative of another person where such payment or gratuity is in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient of the payment or gratuity. FINRA Rule 3220 currently prohibits gifts in excess of $300.00, where the gift or gratuity is in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient. Unlike FINRA Rule 3220, current LTSE Rule 3.291 does not include provisions covering: supervision and record keeping requirements; an exclusion for payments made pursuant to bona fide, written employment contracts; gifts incidental to business entertainment; valuation of gifts; aggregation of gifts; personal gifts; bereavement gifts; de minimis gifts and promotional or commemorative items; donations due to federally declared major disasters; or gifts to a Member's associated persons or individual retail customers. LTSE Rule 3.291 was, therefore, excluded from the 17d-2 Agreement because it was not identical or substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220. To harmonize its rules with FINRA, the Exchange proposes to conform the rule text of LTSE Rule 3.291 to text that is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220 so that it may be incorporated into the 17d-2 Agreement in its entirety.
The Exchange believes that these changes will help to avoid confusion among Members of the Exchange that are also members of FINRA by harmonizing LTSE Rule 3.291 with FINRA Rule 3220. The proposed changes to LTSE Rule 3.291 are designed to enable the Exchange to incorporate LTSE Rule 3.291 into the 17d-2 Agreement, further reducing duplicative regulation of Members that are also members of FINRA. For the avoidance of doubt, LTSE Rule 3.291 would equally apply to Exchange-only Members as the Exchange believes it appropriately protects against improprieties, such as conflicts of interest, that might arise when a Member or person associated with a Member gives items of value to an employee of another person, such as an institutional customer, vendor or counterparty with the hope of strengthening the relationship with the customer.
First, the Exchange proposes to amend LTSE Rule 3.291(a) to increase the gift limit from $100 to $300 per individual per year. FINRA stated that the current gift limit of $100 has been in place since 1992.
[
7
]
FINRA increased the gift limit from $100 to $300 to account for past inflation since 1992 and to account for expected future inflation for approximately ten years, thereby reducing the frequency of future upward adjustments to account for inflation.
[
8
]
Consistent with FINRA's determination, the Exchange believes that a $300 gift limit would continue to permit the exchange of business courtesies while helping to guard against excessiveness, and reasonably reflects changes to purchasing power due to inflation since the gift limit was last raised in 1992 as well as approximately ten years of expected future inflation.
Second, the Exchange proposes to add a new paragraph (d) to LTSE Rule 3.291 that would authorize FINRA staff to conditionally or unconditionally grant an exemption from any provision of LTSE Rule 3.291 for good cause shown, provided that such exemption is consistent with the purpose of the Rule, the protection of investors, and the public interest. Specifically, the Exchange proposes that pursuant to LTSE Rule Series 9.600 (Procedures for Exemptions), FINRA staff, for good cause shown after taking into consideration all relevant factors, may conditionally or unconditionally grant an exemption from any provision of this Rule to the extent that such exemption is consistent with the purpose of the Rule, the protection of investors, and the public interest. This proposed provision mirrors the exemptive relief authority added by FINRA in new Rule 3220(d).
[
9
]
Given the scope of LTSE Rule 3.291, which applies to gifts given to a wide range of recipients where the payment is in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient, and given the diversity of Member sizes, structures, businesses, and distribution models, the Exchange believes it would be useful and appropriate to have the ability to provide relief from a particular provision of the Rule under specific factual circumstances.
Third, FINRA Rule 3220 incorporated published guidance interpreting FINRA Rule 3220, including NASD Notice to Members 06-69,
[
10
]
FINRA's Frequently Asked Questions on Gifts, Business Entertainment, and Non-Cash Compensation,
[
11
]
as well as an interpretive letter regarding bereavement gifts (the “Aly Letter”).
[
12
]
To maintain substantive alignment with FINRA Rule 3220, the Exchange proposes to adopt corresponding Supplementary Material .01 through .09 to LTSE Rule 3.291. Each proposed Supplementary Material section is described below.
Proposed Supplementary Material .01 (Gifts Incidental to Business Entertainment) would state that a gift given during the course of a business entertainment event is subject to LTSE Rule 3.291 unless it is consistent with the requirements of proposed Supplementary Material .04 (Personal Gifts) or .06 (De Minimis Gifts and Promotional or Commemorative Items) which is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220 Supplementary Material .04 and .06. For the purpose of the $300 limit, the cost of the business entertainment event itself would not be included in the value of the gift.
Proposed Supplementary Material .02 (Valuation of Gifts) would require Members to value gifts (other than tickets for sporting or other events) at cost, exclusive of tax and delivery charges, and would require Members to value tickets for sporting or other events at the higher of cost or face value. If gifts are given to multiple recipients, Members must record the names of each recipient and calculate and record the value of the gift on a pro rata, per-recipient basis, for purposes of ensuring compliance with the $300 limit in LTSE Rule 3.291(a). FINRA Rule 3220 at Supplementary Material .02 requires Members to value gifts (other than tickets for sporting or other events) at cost rather than at the higher of cost or market value reduces complexity and subjectivity because market value can be difficult and burdensome to determine, while distinguishing tickets for sporting or other events accounts for the fact that such tickets are commonly purchased on secondary markets at costs that differ from face value.
Proposed Supplementary Material .03 (Aggregation of Gifts) would require Members to aggregate all gifts given by the Member and each associated person of the Member to a particular recipient over the course of the year for purposes of ensuring compliance with the $300 limit in LTSE Rule 3.291(a), and would require each Member to state in its procedures whether it is aggregating all gifts given by the Member and its
(
printed page 69595)
associated persons on a calendar year, fiscal year, or on a rolling basis beginning with the first gift to any particular recipient. The aggregation requirement would not apply to personal gifts under proposed Supplementary Material .04 or to gifts of de minimis value or promotional or commemorative items under proposed Supplementary Material .06 as they are already not subject to the gift limit. This proposed provision which is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220.03 would help ensure that persons who give multiple gifts in a year to the same recipient do not circumvent the gift limit.
Proposed Supplementary Material .04 (Personal Gifts) would state that gifts that are given for infrequent life events (
e.g.,
a wedding gift or a congratulatory gift for the birth of a child) are not subject to the restrictions in LTSE Rule 3.291(a) or the recordkeeping requirements in LTSE Rule 3.291(c), provided the gifts are customary and reasonable, personal in nature, and not in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient. In determining whether a gift is “personal in nature and not in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient,” Members should consider a number of factors, including the nature of any pre-existing personal or family relationship between the person giving the gift and the recipient and whether the associated person paid for the gift. When the Member bears the cost of the gift, either directly or by reimbursing an associated person, the Exchange will presume that such gift is not personal in nature and instead is in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient. This provision is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220 at Supplementary Material .04.
Consistent with FINRA Rule 3220 at Supplementary Material .05 (Bereavement Gifts), LTSE Rule 3.291 at proposed Supplementary .05 separates bereavement gifts from personal gifts. Proposed Supplementary Material .05 would state that bereavement gifts that are customary and reasonable are not considered to be in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient and, therefore, are not subject to the restrictions in LTSE Rule 3.291(a) or the recordkeeping requirements in LTSE Rule 3.291(c). This provision is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220 at Supplementary Material .05.
Proposed Supplementary Material .06 (De Minimis Gifts and Promotional or Commemorative Items), at paragraph (a), would state that gifts of a de minimis value (
e.g.,
pens, notepads, or modest desk ornaments) or promotional items of nominal value that display the Member's logo (
e.g.,
umbrellas, tote bags, or shirts) are not subject to the restrictions in LTSE Rule 3.291(a) or the recordkeeping requirements in LTSE Rule 3.291(c), provided that the value of the gift or promotional item is substantially below the $300 limit. Proposed Supplementary Material .06(b) would state that customary and reasonable solely decorative items commemorating a business transaction are not subject to the restrictions in LTSE Rule 3.291 or the recordkeeping requirements in LTSE Rule 3.291. These provisions are substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220 at Supplementary Material .06.
Proposed Supplementary Material .07 (Donations Due to Federally Declared Major Disasters) would state that donations by a Member or an associated person to any person, principal, proprietor, employee, agent or representative of another person to provide assistance to the individual for losses sustained in a natural event that the President has declared to be a major disaster, such as a wildfire, hurricane, tornado, earthquake, or flood, are not considered “in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient” for purposes of LTSE Rule 3.291(a) and are not subject to the restrictions in LTSE Rule 3.291(a) or the recordkeeping requirements of LTSE Rule 3.291(c). This provision is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220 at Supplementary Material .07 which recognizes that the nature of such disasters is unpredictable and catastrophic.
Proposed Supplementary Material .08 (Supervision and Recordkeeping) would state that the Exchange's supervision rules at LTSE Rule 5.110 require a Member to have a supervisory system reasonably designed to achieve compliance with LTSE Rule 3.291.
[
13
]
To meet these standards, Members would be required to have systems and procedures reasonably designed to ensure that payments and gratuities in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient given by the Member and its associated persons to employees of another person are (a) reported to the Member; (b) reviewed for compliance with LTSE Rule 3.291; and (c) maintained in the Member's records. Such procedures must be reasonably designed to ensure that an associated person who is giving a payment or gratuity is not responsible for determining whether such payment or gratuity is in relation to the business of the recipient's employer. Members are not required to maintain records of gifts that are consistent with the requirements of proposed Supplementary Material .04 through .07. Requiring a person other than the associated person giving the gift to assess the nature of the gift is intended to encourage objectivity in making such determinations and is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220 at Supplementary Material .08.
Proposed Supplementary Material .09 (Gifts to a Member's Associated Persons or Individual Retail Customers) would state that LTSE Rule 3.291 does not apply to gifts from a Member to its own associated persons, or to gifts from a Member or an associated person to individual retail customers. The Exchange believes that proposed Supplementary Material .09 would clarify, and improve awareness and understanding of, the scope of LTSE Rule 3.291 and is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220 at Supplementary Material .09.
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change would promote efficiency without reducing protection for investors and the public interest. The proposed changes to LTSE Rule 3.291 to conform to the rules of FINRA improve transparency, awareness, and understanding of the rule's requirements. The Exchange believes these proposed changes would also help facilitate compliance with LTSE Rule 3.291 and would provide regulatory certainty to Members. Because the Exchange proposes to make conforming amendments that are substantially similar to FINRA's amendments to FINRA Rule 3220, Members that are also FINRA members would continue to be subject to a substantially similar rule when conducting business on the Exchange. In addition, Members that are not FINRA members would continue to be subject to LTSE Rule 3.291 to the extent that such Members conduct business with the public.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change is consistent with the provisions of Section 6 of the Act,
[
14
]
in general, and furthers the objectives of Section 6(b)(5) of the Act,
[
15
]
in particular, in that it is designed to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in
(
printed page 69596)
facilitating transactions in securities, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest.
As noted above, the proposed rule change conforms LTSE Rule 3.291 to FINRA Rule 3220 so that it is substantially similar to FINRA's rule, thereby promoting uniform standards across the securities industry. The Exchange also notes the changes proposed herein align LTSE Rule 3.291 with a recent filing submitted by FINRA and approved by the Commission.
[
16
]
The Exchange believes further that these changes will help to reduce and avoid potential confusion among Members of the Exchange that are also members of FINRA by harmonizing LTSE Rule 3.291 with FINRA Rule 3220. The proposed rule change is designed to enable the Exchange to incorporate LTSE Rule 3.291 into the 17d-2 Agreement, further reducing duplicative regulation of Members that are also members of FINRA. For the avoidance of doubt, LTSE Rule 3.291 would equally apply to Exchange-only Members as the Exchange believes it appropriately protects against improprieties that might arise when substantial gifts or monetary payments are given to certain persons.
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change would promote efficiency without reducing protection for investors and the public interest. The proposed changes to LTSE Rule 3.291 to conform to the rules of FINRA improve transparency, awareness, and understanding of the Rule's requirements. The Exchange believes these proposed changes would also help facilitate compliance with LTSE Rule 3.291.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The proposed rule change is not designed to address any competitive issues but rather to provide greater harmonization among Exchange and FINRA rules of similar purpose, resulting in less burdensome and more efficient regulatory compliance for common members and facilitating FINRA's performance of its regulatory functions under the 17d-2 Agreement. As such, the Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
The Exchange neither solicited nor received comments on the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The proposed rule change is effective upon filing pursuant to Section 19(b)(3) of the Exchange Act
[
17
]
and paragraph (f)(6) of Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
18
]
in that the proposed rule change does not significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; does not impose any significant burden on competition; and does not become operative for 30 days after filing or such shorter time as the Commission may designate.
At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend the rule change if it appears to the Commission that the action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or would otherwise further the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
http://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-LTSE-2026-25 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-LTSE-2026-25. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
http://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of LTSE and on its internet website at
https://longtermstockexchange.com/​
.
Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-LTSE-2026-25 and should be submitted on or before November 25, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
19
]
Sherry R. Haywood,
Assistant Secretary.
