Kanawha River Railroad, L.L.C. (KRR), a Class III rail carrier, has filed a verified notice of exemption under
49 CFR 1150.41
to amend its lease with Norfolk Southern Railway Company (NSR) of, and continue to operate, nine rail line segments totaling 309.45 miles in West Virginia and Ohio (the Lines). The Lines extend between (1) milepost V 381.8 at Maben, W. Va., and milepost V 435.0 at DB (Deepwater Bridge), W. Va.; (2) milepost RR 7.0 at Refugee, Ohio, and milepost RR 116.5 at Hobson Yard, Ohio; (3) milepost WV 125.6 at Conco, Ohio, and milepost WV 253.4 at Cornelia, W. Va.; (4) milepost 0.0 VC at Vaco Junction, W. Va., and milepost 0.84 VC at Deepwater, W. Va.; (5) Hitop RT at milepost TP 0.0 at Charleston, W. Va., and the end of the track at milepost TP 1.0; (6) Jones IT at milepost JT 0.0 at Jones, W. Va., and the end of the track at milepost JT 1.3; (7) milepost VG 0.0 at Virwest, W. Va., and milepost VG 12.5 at Bolt, W. Va.; (8) milepost MY 0.0 at Milam, W. Va., and the end of the track at milepost MY 1.01; and (9) milepost PE 0.0 at Putt, W. Va., and milepost PE 2.3 at Putt End Branch, W. Va.
According to the verified notice, KRR and NSR have recently entered into a Second Amendment to Lease Agreement (Agreement), dated August 17, 2026, updating an extending their current arrangements for KRR's lease and operation of the Lines, dating back to an initial lease agreement entered in 2016 and modified once previously.
See Kanawha River R.R.—Lease Renewal & Operation Exemption With Interchange Commitment—Norfolk S. Ry.,
FD 36028 (Sub-No. 1) (STB served Jan. 4, 2023). KRR and NSR are modifying the base lease terms for a second time, under which modified terms KRR would continue to provide common carrier freight service to customers along the Lines.
KRR certifies that its projected revenues resulting from this transaction will not result in the creation of a Class II or Class I rail carrier but that its current annual revenue does exceed $5 million. Pursuant to
40 CFR 1150.42(e)
, if a carrier's projected annual revenues will exceed $5 million, it must, at least 60 days before the exemption is to become effective, post a notice of its intent to undertake the proposed transaction at the workplace of the employees on the affected lines, serve a copy of the notice on the national offices of the labor unions with employees on the affected lines, and certify to the Board that it has done so. KRR, however, has petitioned for waiver of the 60-day advance labor notice. KRR's waiver request will be addressed in a separate decision in which the Board will also establish the effective date of the exemption.
KRR further certifies that its Agreement with NSR will include an interchange commitment provision regarding interchange with third-party carriers. KRR verifies that the provision was present in the original lease filed in Docket No. FD 36028 and remains in effect. KRR has provided additional information regarding the interchange commitment, as required by
49 CFR 1150.43(h)
.
[
1
]
If the verified notice contains false or misleading information, the exemption is void ab initio. Petitions to revoke the exemption under
49 U.S.C. 10502(d)
may be filed at any time. The filing of a petition to revoke will not automatically stay the effectiveness of the exemption. Petitions for stay must be filed no later than November 10, 2026.
All pleadings, referring to Docket No. FD 36028 (Sub-No. 2), must be filed with the Surface Transportation Board either via e-filing on the Board's website or in writing addressed to 395 E Street, SW, Washington, DC 20423-0001. In addition, a copy of each pleading must be served on KRR's representative, Stephen J. Foland, Fletcher & Sippel LLC, 29 North Wacker Drive, Suite 800, Chicago, IL 60606-3208.
According to KRR, this action is categorically excluded from environmental review under
49 CFR 1105.6(c)
and from historic reporting requirements under
49 CFR 1105.8(b)
.

.

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT).
ACTION:
Supplemental notice of proposed rulemaking (SNPRM).
SUMMARY:
On September 27, 2023 FAA published a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) to amend its Passenger Facility Charge (PFC) regulations to implement congressionally mandated changes to an existing pilot program within the PFC program. FAA also proposed to reaffirm existing program requirements and update or remove obsolete references within the PFC regulations. Following publication of the NPRM and before FAA issued a final rule, the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (the 2024 Act) was signed into law on May 16, 2024. Several sections of the 2024 Act necessitate changes to PFC regulations or modifications to proposals made in the NPRM. As such, FAA now issues this supplemental proposal addressing: PFC turnback reductions; two new PFC-eligible projects; restrictions to PFC-eligible projects; FAA's timeline for review and acknowledgement of notice of intent (NOI) submissions; PFC streamlining review eligibility; and PFC submittal requirements. This proposal aligns with the requirements established by the 2024 Act.

I. Authority for This Rulemaking
FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety is found in
49 U.S.C. 106
, which describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of FAA's authority. Formerly,
49 U.S.C. 106(g)
outlined the duties and powers of the FAA Administrator. The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 reserved
49 U.S.C. 106(g)
and revised section 106(f) to include the Administrator's duties and powers; therefore, in this SNPRM, FAA revised the affected authority citations by citing to section 106(f) instead of section 106(g).
This rulemaking is issued under the authority described in subtitle VII, part A, subpart I, section 40117. Under that section, FAA is charged with prescribing regulations to impose a PFC to finance eligible airport-related projects. This regulation is within the scope of that authority.
This rulemaking is also promulgated pursuant to
49 U.S.C. 106(f)
,
40117
,
40116
,
47106
,
47107
,
47111
,
47114-47116
,
47139
,
47524
, and
47526
.
Finally, this rulemaking is issued pursuant to sections 713, 743, 775, 776, and 782 of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (the 2024 Act),
Public Law 118-63
(May 16, 2024).
II. Executive Summary
A. Overview of the SNPRM
The 2024 Act modified a number of provisions impacting the PFC program regulations. As such, this SNRPM proposes changes to
14 CFR part 158
and certain proposals made in the September 2023 NPRM to align with the 2024 Act's new requirements. Specifically, these proposals address: PFC turnback reductions; two new PFC-eligible projects; restrictions on PFC-eligible projects; FAA's timeline for review and acknowledgement of NOI submissions; PFC streamlining review eligibility; and PFC submittal requirements.
B. Statement of the Problem
The purpose of this SNPRM is to propose changes to the PFC regulations to address requirements enacted by the
(
printed page 69512)
2024 Act. These changes supersede certain proposals included in the NPRM titled “Update and Clarification of the Passenger Facility Charge Regulations” published on September 27, 2023.
[
1
]
Further, the 2024 Act requires changes to additional part 158 regulations that the NPRM did not propose to amend. As such, FAA could not address these new provisions in the final rule resulting from the NPRM, as they require notice and comment as mandated by the Administrative Procedure Act (
5 U.S.C. 553
).
C. Summary of the Costs and Benefits
This SNPRM proposes changes to the PFC regulations to incorporate sections 713, 743, 775, 776, and 782 of the 2024 Act.
FAA examined the SNPRM proposals and identified one that would benefit public agencies that control approximately 138 small-, medium-, and large-hub airports. Specifically, these public agencies would continue using the streamlined application process, shortening FAA's review period from 120 days to 60 days, as outlined in PFC Update 73-20, until the effective date of this final rulemaking. FAA recognizes these gains in efficiency and faster service time to the affected public agencies; however, these benefits, which would continue to accrue to those public agencies, are not quantified or monetized.
FAA also evaluated the cost impact on stakeholders involved in this SNPRM, which includes the public agencies and FAA. FAA determined that the SNPRM changes would have no additional cost impacts to public agencies and FAA.
III. Background
On September 27, 2023, FAA published a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) titled “Update and Clarification of the Passenger Facility Charge Regulations” in the
Federal Register
.
[
2
]
In the NPRM, FAA proposed to amend PFC regulations found in part 158 to implement changes to a congressionally mandated pilot program simplifying the process for public agencies controlling commercial service airports to obtain FAA authority to impose and use PFCs to fund airport development projects. The NPRM was in response to the congressional mandates found in the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2018 (the 2018 Act).
[
3
]
The comment period for the NPRM closed on November 27, 2023 and FAA received six comments.
The 2024 Act renamed the title of
49 U.S.C. 40117
(l) from “Pilot Program for Passenger Facility Charge Authorizations” to “Passenger Facility Charge Streamlining.” This change does not affect PFC program implementation and establishes that the PFC streamlining process is no longer a pilot program.
Need for Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (SNPRM)
The 2024 Act passed on May 16, 2024, which was before FAA published a final rule for the September 2023 NPRM. The 2024 Act included several sections addressing elements of the PFC program. In some instances, such as what types of projects FAA may object to in terms of the PFC streamlining process, the 2024 Act conflicted with the NPRM's proposal and, therefore, requires FAA to put forth new proposals to reflect the 2024 Act's provisions. In other instances, the 2024 Act impacts PFC regulations not contemplated by the NPRM.
IV. Discussion of Supplemental Proposals
In this SNPRM, FAA proposes to:
change PFC turnback reductions,
add two new PFC eligible projects,
remove restrictions to PFC eligible projects,
update FAA's timeline for review and acknowledgement for NOI submissions,
change PFC streamlining review eligibility, and
amend PFC submittal requirements.
FAA also notes in this SNPRM that FAA uses both “notice of intent” (NOI) and “PFC streamlining” when referring to the accelerated PFC review process. With respect to the PFC program, “NOI” is the document submitted by the public agency notifying FAA of the intent to impose, use, or both impose and use PFC revenue. “PFC streamlining” is the process or procedures used to review PFC NOI submittals in an expedited manner within 60 days, versus the 120 days specified in
49 U.S.C. 40117(c)(4)
.
A. PFC Turnback Reductions
Prior to enactment of the 2024 Act, under
49 U.S.C. 47114(f)
, medium- and large-hub airports collecting at a PFC level of $3 or less were subject to a 50 percent reduction of their Airport Improvement Program (AIP) apportioned funds. Medium or large airports collecting at a PFC level greater than $3 were subject to a 75 percent reduction of their AIP apportioned funds.
The 2024 Act decreased these percentages from 50 percent for medium- and large-hub airports collecting at a level of $3 or less and 75 percent for medium- and large-hub airports collecting at a PFC level greater than $3 to 40 percent and 60 percent, respectively.
[
4
]
The 2024 Act also created a new criterion to determine when a small-hub, transitioning to a medium- or large-hub airport, qualifies for a turnback against the airport's apportionment.
[
5 6
]
The new criterion is that an airport must be designated as a medium- or large-hub airport for three consecutive years before a turnback can be applied. For example, a small-hub airport that becomes a medium- or large-hub must remain a medium- or large-hub airport for three years in order for the new criterion to take effect. Accordingly, FAA proposes to amend §§ 158.93 and 158.95 to align the regulatory text with the new statutory requirements.
B. Two New PFC Eligible Projects
The 2024 Act added two new types of projects FAA should consider as eligible airport-related projects.
[
7
]
First, the 2024 Act established eligibility for projects “at a small hub airport for a noise barrier where the day-night average sound level from commercial, general aviation, or cargo operations is expected to exceed 55 decibels as a result of new airport development.”
[
8
]
Second, the 2024 Act added projects that replace “existing workspace elements (including any associated in-kind facility or equipment within or immediately adjacent to a terminal development or renovation project at such airport) related to the relocation of a Federal agency on airport grounds due to such terminal development or renovation project for which development costs are eligible costs under this section.”
[
9
]
FAA interprets the second new project type to include projects related to the relocation of a Federal agency's existing workspace due to an eligible airport development project. The in-kind replacement of that Federal agency's affected workspace elements is now eligible for PFCs. For example, if a terminal development project, funded by PFCs, impedes (by means of physical
(
printed page 69513)
interference) existing Transportation Safety Administration (TSA) workspace elements, this may force the relocation of the workspace elements. The replacement of these workspace elements would be eligible for PFCs.
[
10
]
Accordingly, FAA proposes amending § 158.15(b) to add (b)(10) and (11) to add these two new eligible project types.
C. Restrictions to PFC Eligible Projects
The 2024 Act amended
49 U.S.C. 47139
to repeal emission credit requirements for certain PFC-eligible projects.
[
11
]
Specifically, section 47139 now allows airports to receive emission credits even when they are outside of a nonattainment or maintenance area. As a corollary to that revision, the Act also revised the definition of “airport development” under
49 U.S.C. 47102(3)(K)
and
(L)
to no longer require otherwise eligible airport low emissions projects to be located in air quality nonattainment or maintenance areas. The existing language in § 158.15(b)(8)(i) and (ii) cross-references “airport development” projects (as defined under the new definition in section 47102). As a result, FAA proposes to align the proposed regulatory text with this statutory change by modifying § 158.15(b) to remove the paragraphs referencing those emissions credit requirements. As a result, FAA proposes to remove the following text from existing § 158.15(b): “(8) If the airport is in an air quality nonattainment area (as defined by section 171(2) of the Clean Air Act (
42 U.S.C. 7501(2)
) or a maintenance area referred to in section 175A of such Act (
42 U.S.C. 7505a
), and the project will result in the airport receiving appropriate emission credits as described in
49 U.S.C. 47139
, a project for:”.
Accordingly, under this proposal, projects that would convert vehicles and ground support equipment powered by a diesel or gasoline engine to low-emission technology or acquire low-emission technology vehicles or ground support equipment remain PFC-eligible at any covered airport, as set forth in
49 U.S.C. 40117(a)(3)(A)
. These two remaining provisions would be renumbered as § 158.15(b)(8) and (9) from § 158.15(b)(9) and (10), respectively.
D. FAA's Timeline for Review and Acknowledgement of NOI Submissions
Prior to the 2018 Act, NOIs were submitted by public agencies controlling non-hub airports to FAA for review, and FAA was required to issue an acknowledgment or objection within 30 days of that submission. The NPRM issued on September 27, 2023 retained the 30-day deadline for acknowledgement or objection.
Subsequently, the 2024 Act extended FAA's acknowledgement and objection period for NOI submissions from 30 days to 60 days.
[
12
]
However, the 2024 Act failed to make the corresponding amendment to the paragraph on the authority to impose a charge in section 40117(l)(5). Said provision states: “Unless the Secretary objects within 30 days after receipt of the eligible agency's notice, the eligible agency is authorized to impose a [PFC] in accordance with the terms of its notice under this subsection.”
[
13
]
These two provisions do not align.
It would be administratively difficult and inefficient to manage the PFC program with two different deadlines: a 60-day deadline for FAA to authorize or object to the imposition of PFCs and a 30-day deadline for an eligible Agency to impose a PFC. It would also be nonsensical to develop a program where public agencies could begin imposing PFCs after 30 days of submitting a NOI with the possibility that FAA may object to the NOI within 60 days would create a procedural and administrative burden for both public agencies and air carriers.
[
14
]
For example, under section 40117(l)(5), a public agency may submit a notice of intent to impose and use PFC funds on a project. If FAA does not object within 30 days, the public agency would be authorized to impose, or impose and use, PFC money on that project. Under § 158.43, the public agency, once authorized, notifies air carriers of the latter's obligation to collect PFCs for remittance to the public agency beginning on the charge effective date. However, under section 40117(l)(4)(A), FAA may complete its review and issue an objection after 30 days but within 60 days. If that occurs, the eligible agency is not and never was allowed to impose and use PFC funds for the project. The eligible agency would then be required to return any PFC funds collected and spent for that project to the air carriers, who would then be responsible for refunding passengers.
To spare all entities from unnecessary administrative burden and to avoid any unauthorized collection of PFC funds, FAA proposes in this rulemaking that the 60 days FAA has to issue an objection to a proposed PFC project is also the same length of time that must elapse before an eligible agency is authorized to impose a PFC absent FAA's objection. This proposal is contained in § 158.32(a).
With the additional 30 days, FAA will have the ability to consider complex projects submitted under the NOI process that FAA previously did not have the ability to consider in a 30-day window. Complex projects typically include non-standard projects with multiple components and involve the movement of passengers and baggage. The more components included in a project, the more variables, details, prorations, calculations, and eligibility determinations must be completed. Comparatively, less complex projects include single components, do not involve the movement of passengers and baggage, and are typically prescribed in FAA design and safety standards.
[
15
]
More complex projects require extensive review on the part of FAA to assess the proposal adequately to make a final determination. The 60-day time frame affords FAA more time to review complex projects under the streamlined procedures.
FAA acknowledges that the statutory language in section 40117(l)(5) would, on its own, allow for a public agency to begin imposing fees within 30 days of submission, regardless of FAA action. However, as mentioned above, to avoid administrative waste for the public agencies, air carriers, and FAA, FAA believes it is necessary to align the time period in which a public agency may impose a PFC with the time FAA has to complete a review of the NOI, as extended in the 2024 Act. The FAA recognizes that if it were to adopt a final rule that would allow for the inefficient situation described above, FAA would also need to establish clear requirements on how unauthorized funds must be refunded from both the public agency to the air carrier and from the air carrier to passengers. FAA would expect that
(
printed page 69514)
these requirements would include relatively short deadlines for both refunds, as these funds were not legally authorized, and that they must be refunded in dollars, especially to passengers (
i.e.,
not credits or miles). FAA requests comment on this proposal and whether imposing a consistent 60-day timeframe for both FAA objection and the authorization to begin collecting PFCs would lead to results not discussed in this SNPRM.
In addition, in the NPRM, FAA proposed to create § 158.31 to include regulations for reviews of NOIs. In § 158.31, as proposed in the NPRM, FAA proposed that a public agency would be notified within 30 days by FAA if a project is ineligible for the NOI procedure. Due to changes stemming from the 2024 Act discussed above, FAA modifies § 158.31(a) as proposed in the NPRM to remove the 30-day timeframe for FAA to notify a public agency if a project is ineligible for the NOI procedure.
E. PFC Streamlined Review Eligibility
The 2024 Act established the circumstances under which FAA may or may not object to PFC streamlining.
[
16
]
FAA proposes to amend §§ 158.30 and 158.31 by inserting the allowed and prohibited criteria into these sections.
The NPRM proposed to mirror the policy found in PFC Update 73-20. However, the 2024 Act modified the list of projects ineligible for PFC streamlining found in PFC Update 73-20 and proposed by FAA in the NPRM. This proposal reflects those changes.
The following paragraphs contain a detailed description of the proposals in these two areas.
i. Prohibited Objection, Allowed Objection, and Objected
FAA proposes to align the projects eligible for PFC streamlining with the 2024 Act. Specifically, the 2024 Act created “allowed” and “prohibited” objections for the NOI process. FAA notes that “objection” for the purposes of PFC streamlining differs from an “objection” under the PFC application process. Discussion of the various forms of “objection” continues in the following sections.
ii. Objection to Notice of Intent or Application
FAA's objection to a public agency availing itself of the NOI process differs from an objection to a PFC application. A project in which FAA is allowed to object to the use of the NOI process may proceed to the traditional PFC application process for further review. FAA may object to the application should the application not meet the criteria of the PFC program. FAA is not proposing to change existing eligibility criteria for PFC applications.
Currently, FAA is following PFC Update 73-20 as required by the 2024 Act until the effective date of this final rulemaking. PFC Update 73-20 provides internal guidance on processing applications to impose only, use only, or impose and use PFCs received from small-, medium-, and large-hub airports. PFC Update 73-20 identifies projects that are ineligible for the streamlined process, and the 2024 Act incorporated most of these into the “Allowed” objections described in this SNRPM. FAA does not propose to change its current process except to incorporate “prohibited” and “allowed” sections as described in Section E (iii) and (iv) of this SNPRM.
To distinguish those PFC projects acknowledged under the NOI process from projects approved under the traditional PFC application method found and subject to
49 U.S.C. 46110
as a final agency determination, FAA uses the PFC project statuses to issue a determination on the NOI process only. These three statuses are “Acknowledged,” “Partially Acknowledged,” and “Objected.”
“Objected” is a project status used to reflect FAA's rejection of the imposition of a PFC for a project through NOI or in response to the NOI not following the process of
49 U.S.C. 40117(l)

2. Baseline for the Analysis
The baseline for this analysis remains the same as presented in the 2023 NPRM. Five major sources of airport capital development funding are (1) the AIP; (2) PFCs imposed pursuant to Federal law; (3) tax-exempt bonds; (4) State and local grants; and (5) airport operating revenue from tenant lease and
(
printed page 69516)
other revenue-generating activities, such as landing fees.
[
27
]
The AIP has been providing Federal grants for airport development and planning since the passage of the Airport and Airway Improvement Act of 1982 (Pub. L. 97-248). AIP funding is usually spent on projects that support aircraft operations, such as runways, taxiways, aprons, noise abatement, land purchase, and safety or emergency equipment. The funds obligated for AIP are drawn from the Airport and Airway Trust Fund, which is supported by a variety of aviation user fees and fuel taxes.
Airports use different combinations of these sources to support various needs depending on the individual airport's financial situation and the type of project being considered. Smaller airports, such as those that primarily serve general aviation activities, including private and charter operations, are much more dependent on AIP to meet their capital needs. Larger airports are much more likely to issue tax-exempt bonds or finance capital projects with the proceeds of PFCs.
The PFC program was established in 1990. It was modified in 2005 to institute a pilot program for non-hub airports to streamline the application process in order for them to access the PFC revenues more efficiently and rapidly. The streamlined application process ensures the non-hub airports' PFC applications be treated as a NOI with FAA review and acknowledgment within 30 days instead of issuing a final decision approving or disapproving the application, in whole or in part, in 120 days.
PFC Update 73-20, published in January 2020, gave notice that FAA would review and acknowledge all allowed PFC applications received from small-, medium-, or large-hub airports within 30 days using streamlined procedures. Then, the 2024 Act changed the time allowed for FAA to review and acknowledge notices of intent to 60 days for all eligible airports. This SNPRM proposes to codify this significant statutory change into FAA's part 158 regulations.
According to FAA's National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS), which details the amounts and types of airport development eligible for Federal funding under the AIP over the next five years, there are nearly 3,300 public-use airports within the national airport system. The 2025-2029 NPIAS
[
28
]
published on October 28, 2024 identified 252 non-hub, 74 small-hub, 33 medium-hub, and 31 large-hub airports in addition to 2,910 other public-use airports.
This SNPRM would affect approximately 138 small-, medium-, and large-hub airports. As explained in the preceding paragraphs, proposed changes do not concern either the 2,910 other airports that do not use PFC revenues or the 252 non-hub airports that are currently benefiting from the streamlined application process over the last two decades.

5. Regulatory Alternatives
This rulemaking proposes amendments to the PFC regulations to address statutorily mandated program changes, program oversight improvements, and minor administrative changes, such as removing or correcting obsolete references.
As noted above, FAA is proposing to align the time period in which a public agency may impose a PFC with the time FAA has to complete review of the NOI. FAA believes that such an approach not taken would likely lead to administrative and procedural costs for potential refunds that are likely to outweigh the benefits of public agencies being able to impose fees a few weeks earlier than under the proposed rule. FAA requests comment on this proposal and whether imposing a consistent 60-day timeframe for both FAA objection and the authorization to begin collecting PFCs would lead to costs not considered here. There are no other legally supportable regulatory alternatives to implementing the statutory requirements for the proposed changes. The alternative to rulemaking would be to leave the existing system of FAA orders, guidance, and policy documents in place. However, this is untenable long-term, as such decentralized program requirements and guidance hinder FAA's ability to ensure compliance and transparency. Further, this approach would leave PFC program regulations in place that are not aligned with the 2024 Act, creating potential regulatory ambiguity and inconsistency.

Revise § 158.21 to read as follows:
§ 158.21
General.
A public agency may submit an application and obtain approval from the Administrator to impose a PFC and use PFC revenue, or a public agency may file a notice of intent. This subpart specifies the consultation, notice, and public comment, application, and notice of intent requirements under which a public agency may obtain approval or acknowledgment to impose a PFC and use PFC revenue on a project. This subpart also establishes the procedures for the Administrator's review and approval of applications and amendments, procedures for FAA's acknowledgment of notices of intent, and requirements for use of excess PFC revenue.

§ 158.31
Review of notices of intent.
(a) * * *
(1) A project is ineligible for notice of intent procedures if it:
(i) Establishes significant policy precedent.
(ii) Raises significant legal issues.
(iii) Garners significant controversy, as evidenced by significant opposition to the proposed action by the applicant or other airport authorities, airport users, governmental agencies, elected officials, or communities.
(iv) Raises significant revenue diversion, airport noise, or access issues, including compliance with section 47111(e) or subchapter II of chapter 475.
(v) Includes multimodal components.
(vi) Serves no aeronautical purpose.
(2) FAA must allow a project to follow the notice of intent procedures if it:
(i) is an eligible airport-related project;
(ii) received an FAA-awarded airport grant; and
(iii) the total PFCs collected do not exceed the total cost of the project.

§ 158.95
Implementation of reduction.
(a) A reduction in apportioned funds:
(1) Will not take effect until the first fiscal year following the year in which the collection of the PFC is begun and will be applied in each succeeding fiscal year in which the public agency imposes the PFC, and
(2) Will only be applied to an airport if such airport has been designated as a medium or large hub airport for three consecutive years.
(b) The reduction in apportioned funds is calculated at the beginning of each fiscal year and shall be an amount equal to—
(1) In the case of a fee of $3 or less, 40 percent of the projected revenues from the fee in the fiscal year but not by more than 40 percent of the amount that otherwise would be apportioned under this section; or
(2) In the case of a fee of more than $3, 60 percent of the projected revenues from the fee in the fiscal year but not by

Securities and Exchange Commission

October 30, 2026.
AGENCY:
Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission” or “SEC”).
ACTION:
Notice of applications for deregistration under section 8(f) of the Investment Company Act of 1940.
The following is a notice of applications for deregistration under section 8(f) of the Investment Company Act of 1940 for the month of October 2026. A copy of each application may be obtained via the Commission's website by searching for the applicable file number listed below, or for an applicant using the Company name search field, on the SEC's EDGAR system. The SEC's EDGAR system may be searched at
https://www.sec.gov/​search-filings
.
You may also call the SEC's Office of Investor Education and Assistance at (202) 551-8090. An order granting each application will be issued unless the SEC orders a hearing. Interested persons may request a hearing on any application by emailing the SEC's Secretary at
Secretarys-Office@sec.gov
and serving the relevant applicant with a copy of the request by email, if an email address is listed for the relevant applicant below, or personally or by mail, if a physical address is listed for the relevant applicant below. The email should include the relevant file number. Hearing requests should be received by the SEC by 5:30 p.m., Eastern time on November 24, 2026, and should be accompanied by proof of service on applicants, in the form of an affidavit or, for lawyers, a certificate of service. Pursuant to Rule 0-5 under the Act, hearing requests should state the nature of the writer's interest, any facts bearing upon the desirability of a hearing on the matter, the reason for the request, and the issues contested. Persons who wish to be notified of a hearing may request notification by writing to the Commission's Secretary at
Secretarys-Office@sec.gov
.
ADDRESSES:
The Commission:
Secretarys-Office@sec.gov
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Adam Large, Senior Special Counsel at (202) 551-6720 or
IMOCC@sec.gov
(Division of Investment Management, Chief Counsel's Office), 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-8010.

Abstract:
The Borlaug International Agricultural Science and Technology Fellowship Program (Borlaug) was established in 2004. Borlaug promotes agricultural productivity, food security, trade, and economic growth by providing training and collaborative research opportunities to early and mid-career scientists, researchers, or policymakers from developing and middle-income countries. Since the program's inception, USDA has sponsored almost 1,000 Borlaug Fellows from 69 countries. Borlaug Programs help developing and middle-income countries by providing U.S. based scientific training and collaborative research opportunities to early- and mid-career scientists, researchers, and policymakers.
To achieve its objectives, Borlaug relies on the solicitation for qualified program applicants through a written application. FAS Posts across the globe provide this application to potential Fellows to assist in determining the adequacy of their candidacy alongside FAS Washington. The application is designed to capture the professional status of the applicant, the applicant's personal contact information, and the applicant's suitability for the program. Thus, the Borlaug application is an integral tool to Fellowship Programs Division and FAS' strategic goals at large.
In summary, excluding discrete questions related to program objectives, the Borlaug application collects the following personal information (that may be considered Personal Identifiable Information (PII)): first name, middle name, last name, sex, salutation, birth date, birth city, citizenship country, country of residence, work phone, permanent home address, work address, personal email, work email, emergency contact information (US implementer), and emergency contact information (family contact: name, relationship, home phone, cell phone, and email).

The public reporting burden for each respondent resulting from information collection under Borlaug varies in direct relation to the number of fellowships that each respondent participates in.

Needs and Uses:
The AIE System collects personally identifiable information from individuals requesting access to Army installations. Respondents may include visitors, contractors, service members, dependents, retirees, and civilian employees, as applicable. Information may be collected through an online visitor-registration portal, at a Visitor Control Center, through self-service kiosks, or by authorized personnel at an installation access-control point. Information collected may include identifying and contact information, information from a valid identity credential, and, when required for identity proofing and vetting, biometric and other identifying information.
The Army uses the information to verify an individual's identity; authenticate identity credentials; conduct required vetting against authorized government data sources and access-denial lists; determine fitness for installation access; and issue, manage, or deny local access credentials or visitor passes, as appropriate. The information also supports registration of eligible individuals, maintenance of local access-control records, and implementation of installation physical-security procedures. This collection helps the Army protect personnel, facilities, equipment, and other resources by ensuring that individuals seeking access to Army installations are appropriately identified and screened.
